StreamDictionary.swift:claim.comment:
Takes the first free probe for a key already known to be absent, which is what lets it stop at
the first empty rather than comparing anything.

StreamDictionary.swift:drainPending.comment:
Writes the open entry into storage: an appended value moves into the slot it will live in, a
repeated key's value is assigned into the element it already occupies, that block made unique
first. Both happen inside this call, so no state can be taken between the uniqueness check and
the write -- the whole reason the open value is held here.

StreamDictionary.swift:emptyKeyAddress.comment:
An empty buffer has no base address, and hashing zero bytes never reads one; this gives the
hash a non-null address to be handed rather than a branch inside it.

StreamDictionary.swift:entries.comment:
The key and the hash that guards it, kept in one buffer so a probe reads one cache line and a
retained state copies one thing.

StreamDictionary.swift:hash.comment:
A fixed basis rather than a seeded `Hasher`, which keeps this inside the Embedded subset.
Collided keys degrade to the scan the table replaces, since every step compares a `UInt64`
before bytes. `streamHashBytes` replaced FNV-1a, whose per byte multiply chain was the cost.

StreamDictionary.swift:index.code: public func index(after position: Int) -> Int { position + 1 }

StreamDictionary.swift:init.comment:
Creates an empty streaming dictionary with storage reserved for at least the expected number
of unique keys. Small dictionaries retain the table-free linear scan representation.

StreamDictionary.swift:pendingValue.comment:
The entry being parsed, held inline so the parser's frame points at a slot no other value can
see. It cannot borrow the values array's open element, because a repeated key's open value is
an element the array already holds and a kept state can see. `pendingSlot` is -1 when nothing
is open, an existing slot when the key repeats, and `storedValues.count` when it is new.

StreamDictionary.swift:rebuildTable.comment: Rebuilt from the entries' stored hashes, so growth hashes nothing and never looks at a key.

StreamDictionary.swift:reserveCapacity.comment: Reserves storage for at least the expected total number of unique keys.

StreamDictionary.swift:slot.comment:
On an indexed miss, hands the empty bucket back so insertion does not walk the same probe chain
again. Forced inline, which is worth more than the code it costs: this is a *non-mutating*
method called from inside `_openValue`'s `inout self`, and `Self` is loadable but large.
Measured: out of line the caller stages the whole struct, `memcpy(sp, self, 2164)` per key.
The instance spelling, for the callers that are not on the parse path.

StreamDictionary.swift:storedValues.comment:
Blocked like an array's elements and for the same reason: a snapshot shares the blocks instead
of copying them, and the open value is the array's own inline `pending` slot, so a repeated key
resumes in the slot it already has. Measured: a flat `[Value]` copied the whole value array per
byte on a snapshot-per-byte parse, -58% on the dictionary snapshot rows.

StreamDictionary.swift:table.comment:

sharply past that. Empty below `indexThreshold`, where a scan over `entries` measures the same,
rather than `nil`: an `Optional<ContiguousArray>` cannot be handed to a borrowing probe without
unwrapping, and every unwrap is a retain that makes the buffer non-unique for the next write.

StreamDictionary.swift:value.comment:
A copy of the whole dictionary, for callers that want an escaping snapshot rather than a
single value read by key. The blocks are retained, not copied; the open value is copied,
which is what makes the copy stable while parsing continues.

StreamEnumGeneration.swift:defaultCase.comment:

StreamEnumGeneration.swift:fieldIdentifi.comment:

StreamEnumGeneration.swift:fields.comment: Fields in declaration order, with wildcard names resolved to positional names.

StreamEnumGeneration.swift:partialSyntax.comment:
Generates the partial representation.

Raw-value representations produce `typealias Partial`. `.caseKeyedObject` produces the
partial struct, whose view gains `ResolvedView` and `resolved`, followed by one namespace per
case with associated values, holding that payload's `Partial` and `Value`.

`partialCustomization` and the existing hooks apply to the top-level object partial.
`payloadCustomization` runs for each case with associated values. Its `.generated` result
customizes that payload's `Partial`; `.replacement` emits an entire caller-built payload

library type, so non-empty customizations or hooks throw

StreamEnumGeneration.swift:payload.comment: `nil` for a case without associated values or under a raw-value representation.

StreamEnumGeneration.swift:rawValues.comment:
The strings a `.stringRawValue` case matches. Empty under `.caseKeyedObject`, whose keys are

StreamEnumGeneration.swift:resolvedViewS.comment:
The read side groups every case's view under one switch, so a case can be read mid-stream
without materialising a snapshot. Multi-pattern `case` labels are not implemented for a

`withUnsafePointer(to:)` would dangle once the getter returns.

StreamEnumGeneration.swift:stringMatchBo.comment:

the little-endian word switch also used for object keys, which the compiler turns into a
jump table. Stage two, reached only on a miss, is the prefix chain. A partial carries no
end-of-string signal, so a mid-flight read assumes the shortest case still consistent with
the bytes in hand, by emitting the chain sorted by length.

StreamEventBatchingSink.swift:StreamEven.comment:

skips are not honored.

``streamConvertDecimal(magnitude:exponent:negative:)``, and finally the library's

from 10^-342 through 10^308. It supports finite binary formats with up to 64 bits

Zero is accepted for every exponent.
Other formats can provide their own conversion or use the complete-token fallback.

StreamFieldTable.swift:streamFieldHash.comment:
Murmur3's `fmix64`: the input is already a dense 64-bit word, so there is nothing for a wider
mix to fold in, only avalanche to add so nearby keys don't cluster.

StreamFieldTable.swift:streamFieldTailMa.comment:
Outlined on purpose. Measured inlined (`@inline(__always)`): `PartialSink.key` dropped from 12
callee-saved registers to 6, but the linear scan then stayed out of line as a call to
`streamMatchField`, and typed Twitter / Twitter escaped lost 5-6%. `PartialSink.key`'s table arm
no longer calls this: its scan stops at the first candidate and `matchTableKeyTail` carries the
same compare inline, which is what took the call out of `key`'s loop.

StreamFieldTable.swift:streamMatchField.comment:

prefetcher already has. Longer keys verify their tail on a first-word hit. Takes raw views
rather than the table so nothing is retained on the way in.

StreamFieldTable.swift:streamMatchFieldI.comment:

StreamFrameEntry.swift:_streamWrapperSch.comment:

StreamKeyDecodingStrategy.swift:StreamKe.comment:
How `@StreamParseable` derives the JSON key of each property that does not name its own.

```swift
@StreamParseable(keyDecodingStrategy: .convertFromSnakeCase)
struct Tweet {
  var createdAt: String          // "created_at"
  var inReplyToStatusID: Int?    // "in_reply_to_status_id"
  @StreamParseableMember(key: "full_text")
  var text: String               // "full_text": a key the property names is never converted
}
```

The strategy is the type's own: a member whose type is itself `@StreamParseable` follows the
strategy that type declares. It also applies to an enum without a raw type, to its case names
and associated value labels, which are the object keys `Codable` reads it from.

Where `JSONDecoder` converts each key it reads and compares the result with the declared names,
a stream converts each declared name into the key it expects, once -- as the macro expands for
a built-in strategy, when the type's schema is built for any other -- and matches keys exactly
while parsing. So a strategy costs nothing per key, and the conversions differ from
`JSONDecoder`'s at the edges:

- `userID` is read from `user_id`, where `JSONDecoder` converts `user_id` to `userId` and
  misses.
- A property already named in snake case, `user_id`, is still read from `user_id`.
- Only the conventional spelling of a key matches: `user_ID` does not reach `userID`.

The snake, screaming snake and kebab cases split a name into words as `JSONEncoder`'s
`convertToSnakeCase` does: at an uppercase letter that follows anything else, and one letter
before the lowercase letter that ends a run of capitals (`myURLValue` is `my_url_value`).
Digits stay with the word they follow (`line2Text` is `line2_text`). A leading run of capitals
is one word (`URLValue` is `url_value`), an underscore in the name separates words, and leading
and trailing underscores are kept. The Pascal case uppercases the first letter and keeps the
rest as declared (`userID` is `UserID`).

StreamKeyDecodingStrategy.swift:key.comment:
The key `name` is read from under this strategy.

A custom strategy can build on a built-in one with it:

```swift
.custom { "x_" + StreamKeyDecodingStrategy.convertFromSnakeCase.key(for: $0) }
```

StreamLock.swift:_StreamLock.comment:
Synchronously protects a value on platforms where `Synchronization.Mutex` is available.

This path intentionally includes WASI. A WASI threads SDK supplies `Synchronization`,
whose `Mutex` uses the runtime's thread-aware primitive; treating all WASI builds as
single-threaded would make process-wide caches unsafe under shared-everything threads.

Synchronously protects a value on Apple platforms across the package's deployment range.

New OS releases use `Synchronization.Mutex`. The package still supports releases older
than that module's runtime availability, where it falls back to `os_unfair_lock`.
Compatibility implementation for toolchains that do not provide `Synchronization`.

StreamLock.swift:init.code:
init(_ initialValue: consuming sending Value) {
        self.value = initialValue
        #if canImport(WinSDK)
          self.lock = UnsafeMutablePointer<SRWLOCK>.allocate(capacity: 1)
          InitializeSRWLock(self.lock)
        #else
          self.lock = UnsafeMutablePointer<pthread_mutex_t>.allocate(capacity: 1)
          pthread_mutex_init(self.lock, nil)
        #endif
      }

A macro argument written in a spelling `StreamMacroArguments` cannot read.

Collected rather than emitted. A macro with more than one role reads the same arguments in
each, and has to diagnose from only one of them, or every message is emitted twice.

The stream generation options an attribute writes, read from their spelling, never evaluated.

Reading is best effort: an argument the attribute does not write stays `nil`, as does one
written in a spelling that cannot be read, which adds to `errors` instead. Arguments with other
labels are ignored, so a macro that accepts some of these options beside its own can read its
attribute directly, and every macro reads the same spellings and explains a wrong one the same
way. An explicit `nil` counts as unwritten, as the optional parameters it defaults are.

| Label | Accepted spelling |
| --- | --- |
| `partialMembers:` | `.optional`, `.initialValue` |
| `partialStrings:` | `.streamString`, `.string` |
| `keyDecodingStrategy:` | any expression; see `StreamGenerationConfiguration` |
| `schemaCache:` | any expression; see `StreamGenerationConfiguration` |
| `key:` | a nonempty string literal |
| `keyNames:` | a nonempty array of nonempty string literals |
| `initialCapacity:` | an integer literal, in any radix |
| `completedConversion:` | `Strategy.self` |

A member spelling may name its type (`StreamPartialStrings.string`). A string literal may not
interpolate: `"a\(1)b"` is an error, not the key `ab`.

StreamObjectConversions.swift:conversion.comment:
Generates the members that make the whole type `StreamParseable` against this plan's
partial: `streamPartialValue`, `init?(streamPartial:)`, and `init(orInitial:)`.

Place the result in an extension of the whole type rather than its body: initializers
declared in the body suppress the memberwise initializer. Each field's `name` must name a
stored property of the whole type whose type is the field's `type`.

A configured partial type name other than `Partial` also emits `typealias Partial`.

`init(orInitial:)` falls back to each member's stream initial value, recursively. A
converted member has no such value, so a nonoptional one falls back to its `defaultValue`.

- Parameters:
  - unparsedMembers: Stored properties absent from the partial that have no initializer.
  - partialValueInlining: Inlining for `streamPartialValue`, the only generated member that
    reads the whole type's stored properties. `nil` uses `configuration.inlining`. The plan
    doesn't check that those properties are readable from an inlinable context; a host
    whose properties are less visible than the type passes `.never`.
- Throws: `StreamObjectGenerationError.missingCompletedConversionDefault` for a nonoptional
  converted field without a `defaultValue`, and `.duplicateField` for an unparsed member
  that repeats a name. A plan created with `diagnosedFields:` skips these checks and emits
  recovery syntax instead.

chunk results with `max` rather than a branch (measured: a branch per chunk cost Twitter
discarding 8.7%). A new case takes the next integer.

StreamParseSink.swift:StreamContainerDis.comment:
A sink's answer to a container opening: how it wants the subtree delivered.

Returned from ``StreamParseSink/beginObject()`` and ``StreamParseSink/beginArray()``. The
answer is *advisory*: a deliverer that cannot skip (the batching adapter's replay) delivers the
interior anyway, so a sink answering ``skip`` must still handle it. When the parser honors it,
the interior runs at structural-scan speed with no sink calls. Non-exhaustive, so a
byte-delivering case can be added later.

StreamParseSink.swift:StreamEventBatch.comment: A run of recorded events in document order, delivered together (see `StreamEventBatchingSink`).

StreamParseSink.swift:StreamEventRecord.comment:
One parse event, recorded: what a single sink call would have carried, with its bytes as an
offset and length into one of the batch's byte sources rather than a span.

StreamParseSink.swift:StreamParseSink.comment:
Receives the parser's tokens, one call per token at the lex points (inlined into the parse
loop when specialized). Every span borrows the parser's input or buffer, is invalid once the
call returns, has no readable padding, and ends on a UTF-8 boundary; a key is always whole, and
a number is one call carrying the token and its parsed info.

The container opens return an advisory ``StreamContainerDisposition``. Nothing else throws or
returns: a sink records its failure, which the parser polls through ``streamFailure`` at token
boundaries and reports at the provoking token. Once recorded, later tokens must not clear it.

StreamParseSink.swift:StringInfo.comment:
Where a span delivered to ``StreamStringConvertible/streamAppend(utf8:info:)`` sits in its
string.

Each string brings exactly one call carrying `.begin` and exactly one carrying `.end`, either of
which may also carry bytes, or carry none: a string the parser holds whole arrives as one call
with both. The calls between carry neither, and where they split the string means nothing. A
repeated key writes a second string into the same value, so a value can see `.end`, then
`.begin` again.

StreamParseSink.swift:begin.code: @inlinable public static var begin: Flags { Flags(rawValue: 1 << 0) }
StreamParseSink.swift:begin.comment:
Computed rather than stored, as `NumberInfo.Flags`: an immediate in a client module, not an
addressor call.
The string's opening quote: the first call for this string.

StreamParseSink.swift:beginObject.comment:
Structure. The disposition is deliberately not defaulted: a defaulted returning requirement
silently shadows a conformer's `Void` implementation. Answer `.stream` when in doubt; after a
`.skip` the interior may still arrive, but the matching end call always does.

StreamParseSink.swift:bytes.comment: The bytes the event at `index` would have carried: a key, a string, a chunk, a number.

StreamParseSink.swift:checkIndex.comment:
The accessors below read through raw bases, so they check the index the way `records[index]`
does: an off-by-one at a batch boundary (a key as the last event, its value opening the next
batch) otherwise reads a stale record past the end and builds a span from its offsets. Where a
loop has already subscripted `records` with the same index, as `replay` does, this folds into
that check.

StreamParseSink.swift:commit.comment:
Called when memory the sink's spans borrowed is about to become invalid: at the end of each
parse call and at finish. A sink that deferred work referencing borrowed bytes must complete
it now; when and how much to buffer stays its business. Defaulted to a no-op.

StreamParseSink.swift:digitCount.comment: How many digits the token has, integer and fraction together.

StreamParseSink.swift:end.code: @inlinable public static var end: Flags { Flags(rawValue: 1 << 1) }
StreamParseSink.swift:end.comment: The string's closing quote: the last call for this string.

The byte offset, within the chunk being parsed, just past the event: where the parser
reads the sink's failure, so a rejection reports where the single call path reported it.

The byte offset, within the chunk being parsed, just past the event at `index`, when the
batch's producer recorded it. ``StreamEventBatchingSink`` does not: it reports `0`.

StreamParseSink.swift:exponent.comment: The power of ten `magnitude` is scaled by, clamped to `Int16`.

StreamParseSink.swift:exponent.code: @inlinable public static var exponent: Flags { Flags(rawValue: 1 << 2) }
StreamParseSink.swift:exponent.comment: The token has an exponent part.

StreamParseSink.swift:extra.comment: A `boolean` record's value; an `inline` record's bytes.

StreamParseSink.swift:flags.comment: What the token carries beyond its digits.
What the call carries beyond its bytes.

StreamParseSink.swift:fraction.code: @inlinable public static var fraction: Flags { Flags(rawValue: 1 << 1) }
StreamParseSink.swift:fraction.comment: The token has a fraction part.

StreamParseSink.swift:info.comment: The parsed form of the number at `index`. Meaningful for `number` records only.

StreamParseSink.swift:init.code:

  init(
    replaying recordBase: UnsafePointer<StreamEventRecord>,
    infoBase: UnsafePointer<NumberInfo>,
    count: Int,
    bytesBase: UnsafePointer<UInt8>,
    bufferBase: UnsafePointer<UInt8>
  ) {
    self.recordBase = recordBase
    self.infoBase = infoBase
    self.count = count
    self.bytesBase = bytesBase
    self.bufferBase = bufferBase

StreamParseSink.swift:init.comment:
A batch over caller-owned memory: what `StreamEventBatchingSink` hands its consumer. Not API:
nothing checks that the pointers agree with the records.

StreamParseSink.swift:isWhole.comment: Whether this call is the whole string: it both opens and closes it.

StreamParseSink.swift:key.comment: An object member's key, always whole: unescaped, validated UTF-8.

StreamParseSink.swift:magnitude.comment:
The token's digits, integer and fraction together, read as one integer.

Meaningless when `flags` contains `.overflowed`: more than nineteen digits do not fit, and the
accumulator wrapped. Convert from the token's bytes instead.

StreamParseSink.swift:negative.code: @inlinable public static var negative: Flags { Flags(rawValue: 1 << 0) }
StreamParseSink.swift:negative.comment:
Computed rather than stored, so a client module's `flags.insert(.negative)` is an
immediate and not a call: a `public static let` in another module is reached through an
addressor, and `emitNumber` was making up to four of those calls per number.
The token begins with `-`.

StreamParseSink.swift:number.code: mutating func number(_ bytes: Span<UInt8>, info: NumberInfo)
StreamParseSink.swift:number.comment: One call per number: the whole token and its parsed form.

StreamParseSink.swift:overflowed.code: @inlinable public static var overflowed: Flags { Flags(rawValue: 1 << 3) }
StreamParseSink.swift:overflowed.comment: More than nineteen digits: `magnitude` wrapped and must not be used.

StreamParseSink.swift:replay.comment:
Replays the batch into a sink's per-token methods, stopping at the first recorded failure:
the far side of a `StreamEventBatchConsumer` boundary. Returns `count` when every event was
taken, or the index of the refused one. `.string` records go through
``StreamParseSink/string(_:)``, so a whole-string override is honored.

StreamParseSink.swift:start.comment: Offset of the bytes within `source` (unused for `inline`).

StreamParseSink.swift:string.comment:
The common string: complete in the chunk and escape-free, a zero-copy borrow of the input
delivered as one call. Defaulted through the chunked triple, so a minimal sink implements
nothing extra and an optimized one overrides exactly the hot form.

A whole string is the chunked triple with the middle skipped when empty. `stringBegin`
settles whether the destination accepts strings at all, so the failure check between it
and the chunk keeps a refusal at the opening quote from feeding bytes anyway.

StreamParseSink.swift:stringBegin.comment:
The fallback string form: a value cut by a chunk boundary or carrying escapes arrives as
`stringBegin`, chunks, `stringEnd`. Mandatory for correctness on chunked input.

``JSONParser`` validates every byte of a string value before delivering it, and each span it
delivers is well-formed UTF-8 on its own, here and in ``string(_:)``.

Chunk boundaries carry no meaning. Content before a value's first escape is a zero-copy
borrow of the input; from the first escape on, decoded escapes and the runs between them are
coalesced and delivered per buffer-full (a run at least a buffer long still goes in place, and
an escape straddling a parse call's end arrives as its own chunk).

StreamParseSink.swift:validatedUTF8.code: @inlinable public static var validatedUTF8: Flags { Flags(rawValue: 1 << 2) }
StreamParseSink.swift:validatedUTF8.comment:
The bytes are well-formed UTF-8 on their own: the parser validated them, and the span
neither starts nor ends inside a scalar. A destination may then skip validating them.

Set only by a sink whose producer guarantees it, as ``PartialsStream`` does for
``JSONParser``. A call without it can carry anything.

StreamParseable.swift:StreamParseable.comment:
A value that can expose the partial parsing state consumed from a stream.

You typically do not conform to ``StreamParseable`` directly; instead add the
`@StreamParseable` macro to your struct and let it synthesize the conformance.

The fallback for a partial with nothing worth preserving piecewise (a scalar, or an enum with a
default case). A type with members must not take this: it discards every member that arrived.
These defaults are `@inlinable` so a conformance in another module specializes them rather than
calling the generic entry point with witness tables.

StreamParseable.swift:init.comment:
The strict inverse of ``streamPartialValue``: `nil` when the partial is not complete
enough to describe a whole value.

A member the stream never produced fails, as does one the type cannot represent (a raw value
outside an enum's cases). A member the type declares optional converts to `nil`.

The total inverse of ``streamPartialValue``: members the stream never produced fall back
to their initial values, recursively.

Only absent members default, so a partial carrying just an `id` converts to a value with that
`id`. A type with members implements this member-wise; the blanket default below discards the
whole value when any part is missing.

Disfavored wherever the library adds this to a type it does not own: an unapplied
`String.init` or `Array.init` must keep meaning the type's own `init(_:)`, which takes the
same argument (`stream.map(String.init)` would otherwise be ambiguous).

An uncovered raw value is exactly the failure the strict conversion reports. An enum that would
rather default conforms to `StreamInitializable`, picking up the fallback above.

StreamParseable.swift:streamPartialValue.comment: The partial state that corresponds to the type’s incremental parsing representation.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:Associate.comment:
One associated value of a case, keyed the same way `Codable`'s synthesis keys it: a written
label if there is one, else a positional `_0`, `_1`, ... counted over *every* parameter in
that case (labelled ones included) — verified against `JSONEncoder` directly, since nothing
documents the numbering rule for a mix of labelled and unlabelled parameters.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:SelfRefer.comment:
Finds a type named by `names`. A member type's base is not walked: `E.Kind` is a type nested
in `E`, not `E`. Generic arguments, optionals, arrays, dictionaries and tuples are.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:StreamPar.comment:
Enum support, in the three lowerings tabulated on the `@StreamParseable` docc comment
(`Sources/StreamParsing/Macros.swift`). Only the `String`-raw form can be read *mid-value*: a
key and a number arrive whole, a string arrives in pieces. See `stringRawConversion`.

Generation itself is `StreamEnumGeneration`'s; the macro reads the declaration, diagnoses it,
and places the result. `streamPartialValue` goes out through the member role, the rest through
the extension, matching the struct lowering.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:associate.comment:
The case's associated values, in declaration order. Empty for a case with none — a raw-
value enum can never have any, since Swift itself rejects associated values on a case of
an enum that declares a raw type.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:diagnoseS.comment:
A payload naming the enum, however wrapped (`E?`, `[E]`, `[String: E]`, `Optional<E>`), nests
`Partial` inside itself exactly as `indirect` does, and would build its schema from itself.
Syntactic, like `indirect`: recursion through another declared type is not visible here.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:diagnoseU.comment:
The one place the closed raw-type list can go wrong, caught where it is visible: raw values
on an enum whose raw type the macro did not recognise means it is about to generate the
object lowering for a type that is not written as one.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:explicitK.comment:
Every spelling that resolves to this case, or `nil` for the case name alone, which the enum's
key decoding strategy converts: a raw-less case without `@StreamParseableMember`.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:hasGenera.comment: Only the case-keyed object form generates a `Partial` with a schema of its own.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:isLabeled.comment:
Whether the parameter was written with a label, which decides whether the generated
case-construction call site writes `label:`.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:label.comment:
The label, or the synthesized `_N` — both the generated stored property's name and the
wire-format object key.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:namesAnIn.comment:
Whether the enum says, in its own declaration, what a total conversion falls back to. An
enum that names neither a default case nor `StreamInitializable` cannot conform, and saying
so here beats a missing-requirement error inside an expansion. Deliberately syntactic, so a
conformance added in a far away extension is invisible: the message names the fix.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:reference.comment: The case as written, backticks and all, for use in generated `self = .x` and `case .x`.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:scalarRaw.comment:
The numeric raw types whose `Partial` is the raw value itself, so the conversion is one
`init(rawValue:)`. Closed rather than permissive, because a macro cannot resolve types and
guessing wrong would silently parse a completely different document;
`diagnoseUnsupportedRawType` catches what this list does not claim.

StreamParseableEnumMacro.swift:selfRefer.comment:
`Self`, the bare name, and every qualified spelling the enclosing types allow (`B.E`,
`A.B.E`). The innermost lexical context is usually the enum itself, so it is skipped.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:DiagnosticSin.comment:
Both macro roles run the same readers over the same declaration, so only one of them may
diagnose or every message is emitted twice. The extension role gets a live sink; the member
role gets a discarding one.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:MemberAttribu.comment: A `@StreamParseableMember` and the options it writes.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:access.comment:
The declaration's own access level and `@usableFromInline`, which decide whether an
inlinable member may read it.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:arguments.comment: The options `attribute` writes, with each unreadable one diagnosed.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:attributes.comment:
Keyed off an attribute list rather than a `VariableDeclSyntax`, because an enum case
carries the same attributes in the same place and one reader serves both.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:claimKey.code:
static func claimKey(
    of name: String,
    converting: Bool,
    by strategy: ExprSyntax?,
    in seen: inout Set<String>,
    noun: String = "Key",
    claimant: String,
    at node: some SyntaxProtocol,
    context: DiagnosticSink
  ) {
    guard let key = converting ? StreamDecodedKey(converting: name, by: strategy).knownKey : name,
      !seen.insert(key).inserted
    else { return }
    let origin = key == name ? "" : " (converted from '\(name)')"
    context.diagnose(
      Self.error(node, "\(noun) '\(key)'\(origin) is already claimed by another \(claimant).")
    )
  }
StreamParseableMacro.swift:claimKey.comment:
Claims the key `name` is read from in `seen`, and diagnoses one already claimed. A key a
strategy converts only when the schema is built is unknown here; the built table checks it.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:conformanceCl.comment:
Omitted when the type already states the conformance, which would otherwise be a redundant
one. Read from the declaration rather than the `conformingTo:` list, because a test harness
that expands the macro directly never computes that list.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:conversions.comment:
Both directions come from `StreamObjectGeneration.conversionsSyntax`. The plan comes from
`diagnosedFields:`, so a missing converted default has already been diagnosed here and
recovers as `?? (nil)` rather than throwing.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:declaredAcces.comment:
The getter's access, with `open`, which means nothing on a value type's members, read as
`public`. `private(set)` names only the setter, which no generated member uses.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:declaredType.comment:
`var a, b: Int` annotates only the last binding; the earlier ones share that type. Swift
carries an annotation back only over plain names with neither a type nor an initializer, and
only from a single name that has no initializer itself, so `var name = "Blob", age: Int`
leaves `name` untyped rather than an `Int`.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:diagnoseGener.comment: The same limit for an enum nested in a generic type, which is generic without saying so.

An enum's lowerings still hold `static let`s, which a generic context cannot declare ("static
stored properties not supported in generic types"), so say so instead of expanding into code
that cannot compile. Structs take the generic lowering instead.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:diagnoseIndir.comment:
A recursive case's payload nests `Partial` inside itself ("value type cannot have a stored
property that recursively contains it"), which no amount of generated code can fix.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:enclosingCont.comment:
The innermost lexical context around the declaration, which may itself be first and is
skipped by name, as in `enclosingGenericParameters`.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:enclosingGene.comment: The innermost lexical context may be the declaration itself, which is skipped by name.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:explicitKeyNa.comment:
The keys the `@StreamParseableMember`s write out, or `nil` when the declaration is read from
its name, which a key decoding strategy converts.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:explicitKeys.comment:
The keys `@StreamParseableMember` writes out, or `nil` for `name`, which the type's key
decoding strategy converts.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:generatedAcce.comment:
Generated members have to be at least as visible as the conformance. A private type's are
internal, which its own visibility already limits.

The same, for the declaration as it sits in its lexical context. A type that writes no access
modifier of its own directly inside `public extension` is public, so its conformance is too,
and its generated members have to follow the extension's modifier rather than default to
internal. Only the nearest context counts: a type's members never inherit from further out.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:genericParame.comment:
The generic parameters in scope for a struct's `Partial`: its own, then those of every type
enclosing it. An extension of a generic type declares none it can see, so a type nested there
is still expanded as concrete; nothing syntactic can tell.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:hasDefaultVal.comment:
Whether the declaration supplies its own value. A generated initializer must leave such a
property alone: it is already initialized, and if it is a `let` it cannot be assigned twice.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:hasExistingPa.comment:
Any named declaration, not just a struct: an enum's `Partial` is a typealias in two of the
three lowerings, and a hand written `enum`/`class Partial` has to suppress the generated one
too or the expansion is an invalid redeclaration.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:hasExplicitAc.comment: Whether the getter's access is written at all; `private(set)` alone is not.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:inherits.comment: Whether the declaration's own inheritance clause names `name`, however qualified.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:lastComponent.comment: The last component of a possibly qualified type name, so `Swift.String` reads as `String`.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:memberArgumen.comment:
The first of `members` that writes `name:`, whose value is that option's, `nil` where it is
unreadable. Every later one is diagnosed with `repeated`. An explicit `nil`, which the
optional overloads default to, counts as unwritten.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:memberAttribu.comment:
Every `@StreamParseableMember` in `attributes`, each read once, so an unreadable argument is
diagnosed once however many of the options are then asked for.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:memberPartial.comment:
A member's own `partialStrings:`. Diagnosed beside a `completedConversion:`, whose `Source` is
the storage, and warned where the type spells no `String` for it to reach -- an alias, say,
which keeps `StreamString` whatever is written.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:name.comment:
The bare name, with no backticks: the default JSON key, and the stem of every derived
identifier (`streamObjectMemberSchema_x`).

StreamParseableMacro.swift:partialString.comment: The type's `partialStrings:`, or this member's own `@StreamParseableMember(partialStrings:)`.

StreamParseableMacro.swift:splitConversi.comment:
`streamPartialValue` goes out through the member role, the rest through the extension so a
struct's memberwise initializer survives. Both lowerings generate it first.

StreamParsingError.swift:StreamParsingEr.comment: Signals errors raised by stream parsing operations.

StreamParsingError.swift:incompleteValue.comment:
Thrown by ``PartialsStream/finish()`` when the document ended in a valid state that does not
describe a whole value: ``StreamParseable/init(streamPartial:)`` returned `nil`, because a
member was never produced or holds a value the type cannot represent.

To fill the missing members with their initial values instead, finish with
``PartialsStream/finishPartial()`` and convert with ``StreamParseable/init(orInitial:)``.

StreamParsingError.swift:multipleSubscri.comment: Thrown when more than one iterator attempts to consume an async partials sequence.

StreamParsingError.swift:parserFailed.comment:
Thrown when a stream is used again after its parser failed.

The failure itself is thrown once, from the call that provoked it. After that every call
throws this until ``PartialsStream/reset(to:)`` re-arms the stream.

StreamParsingError.swift:parserFinished.comment:
Thrown when a finished stream receives more bytes or is finished again. Not public: every public
way to finish a stream consumes it or re-arms it, so only the library's own iterators, which
finish a stream they store, can reach a finished one, and they stop before they would.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_any_.comment:
Whether any byte has its high bit set. This is the NEON equivalent of
`simd_reduce_max(value) >= 0x80`, exposed here so every arm64 platform gets the same
two-instruction reduction rather than only Apple platforms where Swift's `simd` module is
available.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_base.comment:
One block: 64 characters to 48 bytes, or 0, writing nothing, if any character is outside the
alphabet.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_base.code: ptrdiff_t stream_parsing_base64_decode_avx2(const void *source, ptrdiff_t groups, void *output);
StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_base.comment:
The base64 decoder's wide tier (`StreamBase64Data`): decodes whole groups of four characters from
`source`, eight at a time, until fewer than eight remain or a block of eight holds a byte outside
the standard alphabet (`=` included), and returns how many it decoded: a multiple of eight, or all
of them when a last, overlapping block covers the remainder. The caller decodes the rest. A block
stores 32 bytes for its 24, so `output` needs room for 8 bytes past the last group's three.
Precondition: `stream_parsing_has_avx2()`.

Each character's sextet, garbage outside the alphabet, and through `valid` nonzero exactly where
the character is in the alphabet.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_clas.comment:
What `consumeSkipRun` (JSONParserSkip.swift) asks of 64 bytes: the bracket bits outside strings,
whether the block holds anything the wide path refuses to judge, and the two carries.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_clas.code:
stream_parsing_skip_classes stream_parsing_classify_skip_block(
    const uint8_t *p, uint64_t in_string_carry, uint64_t ends_odd_carry);
StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_clas.comment:
The two 64-byte block classifiers with the NEON kernels' names, signatures and results, so the
Swift walks are one source on both architectures. Out of line where NEON's are inlined: a
`target("avx2")` body cannot be inlined into Swift built for baseline x86-64. AVX2.c documents
the encoding differences. Precondition: `stream_parsing_has_avx2_block_kernels()`.

`starts` is one word: `(~in_string & ~ws & ~quote) | (quote & in_string)`. Outside a string every
non-whitespace non-quote byte is a candidate, token interiors included (the walk clears them as
its cursor advances). The opening quote is the one byte that is both, so it is added back; the
closing quote drops out, its extent already consumed by whoever visited the opener.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_clas.code:
stream_parsing_structural_classes stream_parsing_classify_structural_block(
    const uint8_t *p, uint64_t in_string_carry, uint64_t ends_odd_carry);

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_find.comment:
Escaped positions: bit i set iff byte i follows an odd-length backslash run. `prev_ends_odd`
carries "the previous block ended inside an odd run" in and out.
Measured: NEON shapes cost +7..+31% per block and a `bs_bits == 0` early-out +0.7..+17.6%;
keep it scalar (PROGRESSION.md, "find_escaped stays scalar").

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_has_.comment:
Whether the two kernels below may be called at all. Resolved on first use and cached. Read
once per process from an out-of-line Swift function, never from an inlined scan loop.

Whether the two block classifiers below may be called: AVX2 plus PCLMULQDQ (the quote parity)
and POPCNT (no longer used by either kernel; every AVX2 part has it). A separate question from
`stream_parsing_has_avx2` so a (hypothetical) AVX2 part without either keeps the validator and
the string scanner. Resolved on first use and cached with the same probe.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_load.comment:
The bytes `s[0, n)`, 0 < n < 16, in the low lanes of a vector with every other lane zero, read
without touching a byte outside them: two overlapping 8-byte loads, two 4-byte loads, or the
first, middle and last byte. Only a run that sits within the first sixteen bytes of its buffer
comes here (see `stream_parsing_utf8_validate_neon`), so the size-class branches stay cold.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_move.comment:
One bit per byte of a 64-byte block, ascending. `vshrn` folds a 16-lane vector to a nibble per
lane and is the right tool for "which lane"; this is the other question -- four vectors down to
one word -- and the bit-weight-plus-pairwise-add form is what NEON has for it.

The same word from a block loaded with `vld4q_u8`, where vector j lane i holds byte 4i + j: three
shift-right-inserts stack the four vectors' top bits into one lane's high nibble (byte 4i + 3 at
bit 7 down to 4i at bit 4), a fourth copies that nibble into the low half, and `shrn #4` packs
lane pairs into bytes -- byte k of the word is bits 8k ... 8k + 7, in order. Five vector
instructions against `movemask4`'s seven, and only bit 7 of each lane is read, so a class the
lookup already leaves in bit 7 needs no compare at all. Measured: see the skip classifier.

The arm64 movemask Swift cannot spell: `vshrn_n_u16` takes an immediate, so it does not import
and no portable SIMD operator lowers to it. Lane n of the input lands in nibble n of the result,
0xF where the byte was 0xFF. Measured: one `shrn` + `fmov` answers both "any hit" and "which
lane" against a `uminv` chain or a `umov` ladder; keep it a leaf returning a scalar, not a struct.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_pow1.comment:
10^k as an integer for k in 0 ... 16: `streamAccumulateLeadingDigits` scales the magnitude by
10^count for the 0...7 numerals it takes from a partial word. A function-local table rather
than a Swift array, which would be a lazily initialised global.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_pref.comment:
Quote parity: bit i becomes the XOR of bits 0...i, which turns a mask of unescaped quotes into
"is byte i inside a string" -- the opening quote included, the closing one not. One carryless
multiply by all ones where the target has it, six shift-xors where it does not.

or control byte in `[from, to)`, or `to`, and reports through `out_non_ascii` whether any byte

stream_parsing_unescape_result stream_parsing_unescape_blocks(
    const uint8_t *source, ptrdiff_t count, uint8_t *target, ptrdiff_t room);
StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_unes.comment:
Copies string content from `source` to `target` in whole 64-byte blocks, decoding escapes
(`\uXXXX` and surrogate pairs included) and validating UTF-8 (with
`stream_parsing_utf8_block_errors` and the kernel's own copy of the three tables). Nothing past
`count` is read and nothing past `room` written; bytes past `produced` in the target are junk.
Everything up to `consumed` is valid UTF-8 ending on a sequence boundary.

Byte `nibble` of the kernel's copy of UTF-8 table `table` (0: previous byte's high nibble,
1: its low nibble, 2: the current byte's high nibble), for the test that holds it to the
Swift tables.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_utf8.comment:
The UTF-8 validator's block kernel, whole: three nibble table lookups ANDed (Keiser and Lemire's
special cases), XORed with 0x80 where a three or four byte lead requires a continuation; nonzero
lanes are errors. The three "previous byte" views are the caller's: in the run loop, unaligned
loads at i-1/2/3; for a block with nothing before it, `ext` against zero (below).
Measured: composed in Swift 2.6x slower, `ext`-shifted views in the run loop 10% slower; keep
the C kernel.

The block kernel for a block with nothing before it: the three "previous byte" views are the
block itself shifted in from a zero vector (`ext`), so lanes ahead of the block read as ASCII --
the same thing a zero-padded scratch said, without the bytes going through memory.

StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_utf8.code: int stream_parsing_utf8_validate(const void *base, ptrdiff_t from, ptrdiff_t to);
StreamParsingShims.h:stream_parsing_utf8.comment:
1 = valid, 0 = invalid. `from`/`to` bound the run; nothing before `from` is part of a sequence
and no sequence may run past `to`, matching `streamValidateUTF8Scalar`.
Precondition: `stream_parsing_has_avx2()`.

The arm64 validator's whole run loop: 1 when `[from, to)` is well formed UTF-8 in full, 0 when
not. Nothing before `from` is part of a sequence and no sequence may run past `to`.

Contract on memory: every byte in `[0, to)` of `base` is readable, and nothing past `to` is read.
Every caller passes the start of the chunk, of the parser's own buffer, or of the one-byte
`parse(byte:)` scalar as `base`, so this holds at all of them.

No byte goes through memory. The first block's "previous byte" views come from `ext` against
zero; a run shorter than a block is the sixteen bytes ending at `to` with the lanes before `from`
cleared; the tail is the sixteen bytes ending at `to` again, overlapping bytes already checked,
which is harmless because each lane's views are still the bytes truly before it. Measured
against a 32-byte zero-padded stack scratch, which compiled to `memcpy` calls whose byte stores
then fed 16-byte reloads, spilled four vector registers around the calls, and armed the stack
protector.

StreamPartialConversion.swift:StreamPars.comment:
What a macro-generated initializer is written out of, so the type checker supplies the target
type. `typeOf` is never called but must stay: binding `T` to the declared type makes a wrong
`partialTypeName` a compile error, not a silent misparse (the `[String?]` double-optional bug).
A closure, not a `KeyPath`, for Embedded; an unwrapped member's argument promotes to `.some`.

StreamPartialConversion.swift:_streamSto.comment:
Strict, for a member the partial stores as the model spells it (`partialStrings: .string`):
nothing to convert, so only absence fails. The macro maps a container's storage to the
member's type before the call; binding `T` still makes a wrong storage spelling a compile error.

Total: an absent stored member falls back to `initial`, which the macro writes as the member
type's empty value (`""`, `[]`, `[:]`, `nil`).

StreamPartialConversion.swift:_streamVal.comment: Strict: an absent member fails the whole conversion.

Total: an absent member falls back to its initial value, recursively.

The fallback is on `T.Partial`, not `T`: every `Partial` is `StreamInitializable`, so any
parseable member supplies its own default and this conversion is available on every type.

StreamScanners.swift:StreamStringRun.comment:
The string scanner already loads every byte needed to find a quote, escape or control byte.
Carrying the high-bit observation with the end index lets validated string values skip a second
ASCII-only pass. The flag is exact: bytes after the first terminating lane are masked out.

StreamScanners.swift:StreamUTF8ErrorClas.comment:
Keiser and Lemire's lookup validator ("Validating UTF-8 In Less Than One Instruction Per Byte"):
every error is visible in two adjacent bytes plus one structural fact, so three nibble-indexed
error-class tables ANDed and XORed validate a sixteen byte block at once. It answers only valid or
not; the scalar walk locates the byte, keeping error offsets where `ErrorOffsetTests` pins them.

StreamScanners.swift:_streamPaddedLeadin.comment:
A generated matcher switches on the leading word, then checks the count and any remaining
words. The count is load bearing even below eight bytes: JSON keys can contain a decoded NUL,
which is otherwise indistinguishable from the zero padding.

StreamScanners.swift:carry.code: @usableFromInline package static let carry: UInt8 = tooShort | tooLong | twoContinuations

StreamScanners.swift:streamAccumulateDig.comment:
Accumulates a digit run into `magnitude`, returning the run's end, with no per-digit loop when
`to >= 8`. Each eight bytes before `to` get one SWAR class test that serves both outcomes: all
numerals is a full block, converted from the same subtraction; otherwise the run ends inside the
word and its leading numerals are the last step. With fewer than eight bytes left, the eight
*ending* at `to` are shifted down so the remaining bytes are the low ones (the zeros shifted in
end the run) -- already consumed input, as in the short integer kernel -- and only a buffer
shorter than eight bytes takes the byte loop. Replaces a byte loop of dependent multiplies with
a data-dependent exit per segment, and the SIMD block whose class test could not be reused.

StreamScanners.swift:streamAccumulateLea.comment:
The numerals at the start of an eight-byte word (its low bytes, in memory order), up to the
first byte that is not one, accumulated into `magnitude` with one multiply; returns how many.
`biased` and `nonDigit` are `streamDigitClass(word)`; the caller guarantees `nonDigit != 0`, so
the count is 0...7.

The numerals' own lanes of the class test's subtraction are their digit values, so they are
shifted to the top of the word (the right alignment the eight-digit conversion wants, zeros
below) rather than masked; the shift is split in two so a count of zero shifts everything out
instead of masking to a shift of nothing.

StreamScanners.swift:streamBytesAreASCII.comment:
Whether no byte has its high bit set. Ored sixteen at a time and tested once at the end: a
caller that finds a non-ASCII byte decodes the whole text anyway, so stopping early saves little.

StreamScanners.swift:streamBytesEqual.comment:
Byte equality, sixteen bytes at a time. The lanes are xored and the difference read as two words
rather than compared into a mask: `any(mask)` lowers to an out-of-line reduction call, which is
the same reason `streamIsEightDigits` spells its all-lanes test by hand.

StreamScanners.swift:streamCompareBytes.comment:
Lexicographic byte ordering, sixteen bytes at a time. The return follows `memcmp`: negative,
zero or positive according to the first unequal byte. Locating that byte from the xor keeps
the agreeing prefix in registers rather than walking the underlying memory a second time.

StreamScanners.swift:streamDigitClass.comment:
One subtraction per word: `biased` is every byte minus `'0'`, `nonDigit` has bit 7 set in the
first byte that is not a numeral -- exactly, because a byte below `'0'` borrows, and a lane at or
above `0x8A` carries, only into the bytes *above* it. Bytes above the first non-numeral may be
flagged spuriously, which nothing here reads.

StreamScanners.swift:streamEightDigitVal.comment:
Eight digit values, most significant in the lowest byte, as one integer: the short integer
kernel's three multiply-shift stages.

StreamScanners.swift:streamFirstDifferen.comment:
The offset of the first unequal byte, or `count` when every byte agrees: `streamCompareBytes`'s
walk, answering where rather than which way.

StreamScanners.swift:streamFirstHitLane.comment:
The lowest lane where `mask` is set, or 16 when no lane is: the portable spelling of the movemask
idiom. Mask bytes are 0xFF or 0x00, so read as two little-endian words each lane owns a byte and
the lane is the trailing zero count over eight; two empty words give 8 + 8 == 16, one past the end.
Measured: as `low != 0 ? ... : ...` LLVM's X86CmovConverterPass re-branches the `cmov`; keep this.

StreamScanners.swift:streamFirstHitLaneN.comment:
The arm64 spelling of the same operation. `stream_parsing_movemask_u8` uses `vshrn_n_u16`,
which Swift cannot import directly because its shift is an immediate. Each mask byte becomes
one nibble, so the first set lane is the trailing-zero count divided by four. A zero mask's
count is 64 and therefore answers 16, matching the portable function.

StreamScanners.swift:streamHashBytes.comment:
A key's hash, vectored where the length allows it. Two accumulators fed from one SIMD16 load,
replacing FNV-1a's per-byte multiply chain; the tail is a bounded word ladder for the reason
`streamPaddedWord` documents. Nothing here is serialised, so the word order only has to agree
with itself — a key of a given length always takes the same path.

StreamScanners.swift:streamHexQuad.comment:
Four hex digits in one general-purpose register, so the result never crosses from a vector
register. Each byte's range is tested by adding a bias that carries into its top bit exactly when
the byte is at or past a bound -- no carry leaves a byte below 0x80, and a byte at or above 0x80
fails on its own top bit whatever it carried into its neighbour. The 0x20 bit folds case for the
letter test only (digits already carry it, and folding them would admit 0x10...0x19). A digit's
nibble is its low four bits; a letter's is its low four bits plus nine, and bit 6 is set on
letters only. Returns nil unless all four are hex, so the caller can fall back rather than having
to report which one was not.

StreamScanners.swift:streamIsEightDigits.comment:
`all(mask)` lowers to an out-of-line `SIMD.max()` call, which also forces a stack frame onto
the accumulate loop below, so the all-lanes test is spelled as one 64-bit compare over a 0/1
lane vector. The comparand is byte-symmetric, so the bitcast is endian-independent.

StreamScanners.swift:streamMaskBytes.comment: A mask as bytes, 0xFF where set: the mask's own storage, read as unsigned.

StreamScanners.swift:streamNumberClassHi.comment:
bit0 digit-possible, bit1 dot-possible, bit2 plus-possible, bit3 dash-possible, bit4
E/e-possible. Indexed by a byte's high nibble.

StreamScanners.swift:streamNumberClassLo.comment:
Indexed by a byte's low nibble. Low nibble 5 carries both digit ('5' is 0x35) and E/e ('E' is
0x45, 'e' is 0x65) bits; the high nibble table resolves which one applies, or neither — '%' is
0x25, whose high nibble carries none of the bits low nibble 5 offers.

StreamScanners.swift:streamNumberRunEnd.comment:
Finds the first byte outside the number token class: the ten numerals, '.', 'e', 'E', '+', '-'.
The scan is greedy -- placement is the whole-token parse's business -- which keeps it stateless
and lets one vector test all six conditions per lane. On arm64 that is two nibble-indexed table
lookups (`ldr, ushr, tbl, and, tbl, cmtst`); trap: on a bitcast mask `all()` silently deoptimises.

StreamScanners.swift:streamNumberRunEndP.comment:
Reachable with the arm64 fast path forced off, so tests can hold it to the same oracle as the
vector path on a machine that has both.

StreamScanners.swift:streamPaddedWord.comment:
Eight key bytes as one little-endian word -- the first thing a generated matcher does to a key.
The load must stay bounded by the span: a key span is a borrow into the parser's input and there
is no padding behind a key to overread into. Under eight bytes it is a halving ladder, not a
vector: NEON has no masked load, and most JSON keys (`id`, `text`, `user`) land in that tail.

StreamScanners.swift:streamParseEightDig.comment:
The same tree over digits that are already biased. The short integer kernel below masks its
junk lanes to zero before converting, and zero is the digit it wants them to be, so it cannot
hand this function ASCII.

The classic eight-byte conversion as a SIMD lane tree: '0'-biased bytes combine pairwise, the lane
count halving each stage and widening only where the next place value needs it. Every stage is
exact, so the block agrees with the scalar loop and only the accumulate wraps, keeping
overflowed magnitudes congruent mod 2^64. Measured: 7-13% over the SWAR form it replaced.
`streamAccumulateDigits` no longer calls it: its SWAR class test per word is also the
conversion's input (PROGRESSION.md, "Landed: a number's digit runs finish in one SWAR word").

StreamScanners.swift:streamScannerVector.comment:
SIMD16 beat scalar, SWAR and SIMD32 at every run length on arm64 (table in PROGRESSION.md):
NEON registers are 128 bits, so SIMD32 lowers to two operations plus a recombine.

StreamScanners.swift:streamShortInteger.comment:
An unsigned integer of one to eight numerals, parsed whole with no loop and no data dependent
branch, or `nil` if the token is not that shape; the class test doubles as the shape test. The load
is the eight bytes *ending* at the token -- already consumed input, so `end >= 8` makes it safe, and
right alignment makes the masked-off bytes leading zeros. Mask before bias, or `0x30` borrows in.

StreamScanners.swift:streamSimpleEscapeT.comment:
A direct byte-to-byte map for JSON's eight simple escapes; the parser handles `u` first. Zero means
"not a simple escape", and no valid one decodes to NUL, so the sentinel needs no validity table.
A `StaticString` puts the 128 bytes in read-only storage, as the one-allocation path and Embedded need.
swift-format-ignore

StreamScanners.swift:streamStringRunNarr.comment:
The SIMD16 continuation, reachable when AVX2 is absent. A second copy of the loop above rather
than a shared body, for the reason the UTF-8 validator's two variants already document.

StreamScanners.swift:streamStringRunStag.comment:
`streamStringRun` that also copies what it scans: each block is stored to `staging` from the
register the terminator test reads, so string content bound for a buffer is read once and never
goes through a variable-length `memmove`. Whole blocks are stored, so the bytes after a
terminator's lane are junk the caller does not count: `staged` is how many bytes from `from` on
are good. `room` is how many bytes `staging` can take; a block is staged only while all sixteen
of its bytes fit and lie before `to`, and the rest of the run is scanned without a copy, for the
caller to move however it moved runs before.

StreamScanners.swift:streamStringRunWide.comment:
Out of line on purpose, and this is where the availability check belongs: reading `streamHasAVX2`
is a lazy-init accessor call, affordable once per escalated run and ruinous at the entry of the
inlined scanner (measured `CITM catalog` -9.9%). Without AVX2 the scan continues at SIMD16 rather
than failing, which is what the narrow twin below is for.

StreamScanners.swift:streamUTF8CurrentHi.comment: Indexed by the high nibble of the current byte.

StreamScanners.swift:streamUTF8PreviousH.comment: Indexed by the high nibble of the previous byte.

StreamScanners.swift:streamUTF8PreviousL.comment: Indexed by the low nibble of the previous byte.

StreamScanners.swift:streamUnicodeEscape.comment:
`\u` as one little-endian halfword. The second escape of a surrogate pair is the one place two
known adjacent bytes are tested, so it is one load and one compare rather than two of each.
Built from the byte constants rather than written as a literal, and read back through
`UInt16(littleEndian:)`, so it does not depend on the host's byte order.

StreamScanners.swift:streamWhitespaceBit.comment:
JSON whitespace as a 64-bit set indexed by the byte itself: tab, line feed, carriage return and
space. Swift's smart shift yields zero on over-shift, which is what makes indexing by a raw byte
correct (arm64's own shift masks the amount to six bits and would alias byte 64 onto byte 0);
the defence costs one `cmp`/`ccmp` pair against 63.

StreamScanners.swift:streamWhitespaceEnd.comment:
One compare in front, scans out of line: every JSON whitespace byte is <= 0x20 and every byte that
may legally follow one is > 0x20. The inlined body must stay this small. Measured: inlining the
vector body or peeling a one-byte run here cost -18%/-34% on whitespace-free escape-dense
documents, and routing the byte-fed path (`to &- from == 1`) through the vector cost twitter -20%.

The run end and the byte that ends it, for callers that dispatch on that byte: `streamWhitespaceEnd`
would load it, test it and throw it away, and every caller would reload the same address.
The byte is meaningless when `end == to` and is reported as zero there; every caller must test
that first.

StreamScanners.swift:streamWhitespaceMis.comment:
Which lanes of a block are not whitespace. On arm64 one table lookup and a compare rather than four
compares ORed: 0x20, 0x09, 0x0A and 0x0D have distinct low nibbles, so a nibble-indexed table hands
back the one whitespace byte a lane could be. The filler must be 0x00, not 0xFF -- a filler must
differ from every byte that indexes it, and 0xFF's low nibble matches itself at entry fifteen.

StreamScanners.swift:streamWhitespaceRun.comment:
Kept out of line deliberately: measured, inlining the vector body into the parse loop cost 18-35%
on whitespace-free escape-dense documents -- the loop's register pressure, not the scan. The
structural and skip runs take the inline twin below. LOCKSTEP: `streamWhitespaceRunEndInline` is
this body character for character, and only `StreamScannerTests` exercises this one.

The same body as `streamWhitespaceRunEnd`, forced inline for `consumeStructuralRun`, where the call
was 16% of `twitter`. LOCKSTEP: a fix to either body belongs in both. Measured: `@_transparent`
must stay on the whole chain (the step, `streamWhitespaceEndByte`, this) because it inlines before
the size heuristic votes; the hit test is the shim because `any`/`all` on a composed mask deopts.

StreamSchema.swift:KeyRouting.comment:
Where a key arriving at this schema has to go, precomputed into one byte so the common case --
a subtree the destination has no field for, 52% of `twitter.json`'s keys for a typical model --
never loads and calls a closure to reach `{ _ in -1 }`. Measured: 17 ns against 4.6 ns for a
bare function pointer; keep the byte, one load and one switch.

StreamSchema.swift:StreamContainerPartia.comment:
A partial that can receive an incoming container when stored as a field.

The entry operation lives on the resolved partial type, so aliases and generic wrappers do not
need to expose their shape in source syntax. A partial whose storage is described directly by
its ``StreamPartial/streamSchema`` can use the default implementation.

StreamSchema.swift:StreamFrame.comment:
The destination a hand-written ``StreamSchema/enterField`` pushes for a container it opens: the
address of the value being written, and which schema routes tokens into it.

The schema is named by its position in the entering schema's ``StreamSchema/children`` rather
than handed over, because the sink borrows it without retaining it: the entering schema owns
its children, so a frame cannot name a schema that is freed while the parse still writes
through it. ``reentering`` names the entering schema itself, for a container shaped like its
parent. A position outside `children` stops the program.

StreamSchema.swift:StreamParseableObject.comment:
Refines `StreamContainerPartial` so a nested object field's schema is hoisted by its parent
exactly as a container field's is. Reading `T.streamSchema` per occurrence builds a fresh schema
for any hand-written conformance, leaving the frame as its only owner — invisible while a frame
retains its schema, fatal now that a frame borrows it.

StreamSchema.swift:StreamPartial.comment:
The storage a stream writes into: a partial value that describes how the parser routes tokens
into it.

``StreamParseable/Partial`` is always one. A model type (`Post`) has a generated partial
(`Post.Partial`) whose members are all optional; a scalar or a streaming collection is its own
partial (`Int`, `StreamArray<Int>`). You rarely name this protocol: reach for
``StreamParseable``, which every partial type also conforms to with `Partial == Self`.

The schema has to be a protocol requirement rather than a macro overload, because a function
generic over the stored type -- `partials(of:from:)` -- cannot pick an overload on its behalf.
Kept separate from ``StreamParseableObject`` so the constrained `_streamFieldRoute` cannot
route a `String` field.

StreamSchema.swift:StreamRouteBits.comment:
The packing of a frame's route word: the leaf route in the low byte, the element kind above
it, the element's optionality above that. `elementKindMask` is non-zero exactly when a scalar
arriving at the frame has a typed slot, which is the one test the scalar entry points make.

StreamSchema.swift:StreamSchema.comment:
`@unchecked` for the raw views the schema keeps of its field table and of its element schema
below: immutable pointers into storage the schema itself owns for its whole lifetime, read and
never written after `init`.

StreamSchema.swift:Usage.comment:
Which of a type's schemas is meant: the one for where the parser meets a value, relative to
whatever holds it.

Each usage has its own requirement, which defaults to ``root``'s, so the schemas differ only
for a type that says otherwise -- `Optional`, whose element and value slots are opened already
materialised. ``StreamSchemaCache`` keys each entry by type and usage.

StreamSchema.swift:_StreamKeyDispatch.comment: Kept separate from KeyRouting so instrumentation does not add cases to scalar hot paths.

StreamSchema.swift:_StreamLeafRoute.comment:
A closed byte naming the exact standard-library/storage pairings `PartialSink` can see through.
Everything else stays `.generic` and goes through the schema closures, so a custom conformer is
always correct and a fast route is always an explicit benchmarked choice. A scalar schema carries
a `value...` case only so a container builder can map it; only container cases reach a frame.

StreamSchema.swift:_streamNullValue.comment:
What a whole-value `null` writes into a member of this type, or `nil` for a type that has
no null of its own, whose optional member is cleared instead.

The macro decides this from a member's declared type (`_streamApplyNull`'s overloads) except
where that type is a generic parameter's `Partial`, which the overloads cannot see through.
Defaults to ``StreamNullable/streamNullValue()`` for a nullable type, so `Box<Int?>` takes a
`null` as `.some(nil)` -- a present null, as `Codable` reads it -- where a concrete `Int?`
member, whose optionality is written, has only the one `nil`.

StreamSchema.swift:_streamObjectMemberPr.comment:
Makes the storage of a member of this type ready for ``streamObjectMemberSchema`` to write
through, before the sink pushes a frame over it; runs once per container occurrence. `nil`
for a type whose storage is its own value, which is every type but `Optional`, which
materialises its payload here. The table stores it as the member's `prepare`.

StreamSchema.swift:_streamOpensByConstru.comment:
Whether a container opens a slot of this type by constructing ``streamInitialValue()``
rather than copying the template its schema hoisted.

True for the `Partial` the macro generates for a generic struct and for `StreamArray` and
`StreamDictionary`, and `false` for everything else. A bound generic struct's copy is not emitted field by field: it fetches the type's
metadata and calls its value witness, which walks the fields through metadata too. Measured
on the matched Twitter model, one generic level cost 1.5% per element opened that way, while
constructing is the specialised `init`'s inline stores. A concrete `Partial` keeps the
template: its copy is inline, and its `streamInitialValue()` is itself a copy of one.

StreamSchema.swift:_streamOptionalArrayS.comment:
The macro emits this and `_streamOptionalDictionarySchema` for a `[T?]` / `[String: T?]` member,
spelling the name by interpolation (`containerSchemaExpression`), so a grep for the full name
finds only this declaration. A root or bound generic reaches the same shape through
`Optional.streamArrayElementSchema` instead.

An array whose elements are optional. The element is opened as `.some` rather than `nil`, which
is the whole reason the element schema above can write straight through: `Optional`'s own
`streamInitialValue()` is `nil`, and applying the wrapped type's schema to the `.none`
representation is a write through a pointer to a value that is not there.

StreamSchema.swift:_streamOptionalElemen.comment:
The schema an optional element or dictionary value is written through. Exactly two things differ
from the wrapped type's own schema -- everything else is the *identical* closure value, so a token
costs one schema call, not two. Nothing checks for `nil` first, because the container opened the
slot materialised (73.5 ns/element against 32.9 here); and a null naming the value clears it.

StreamSchema.swift:_streamSIMD2DoubleSch.comment:
Durable exact schemas let the sink open a SIMD element directly from a known parent array
without constructing a frame whose schema is its only owner.

StreamSchema.swift:_streamSIMD2Schema.comment:
A SIMD value is a JSON array whose element count and storage are known before parsing begins, so
there is no cursor, pending element or allocation in the value. `PartialSink` keeps the next lane
in the frame's `pendingField` and, for a scalar the library knows (`elementKind`), writes lane `i`
at `storage + i * stride` itself; only a custom scalar reaches `applyNumber` with the lane.

StreamSchema.swift:_streamStringSchema.comment:
Shared by the root conformances below and by the macro's `_streamSchema(for:)` overloads, so
the two cannot describe the same type differently.

StreamSchema.swift:appendElement.comment:
Appends an element and returns its slot, which the sink writes through ``elementSchema``.
Arrays only. `index` is the element's position, which a dynamic array ignores.

StreamSchema.swift:applyBoolean.code: public let applyBoolean: @Sendable (UnsafeMutableRawPointer, Int32, Bool) -> StreamApplyResult

StreamSchema.swift:applyString.comment:
Each reports what the destination did with the token: `.unsupported` for a matched field with no
destination for this token kind (how the sink tells a type mismatch from an absent key),
`.capacityExceeded` for full bounded storage. A result rather than a throw, because the check
after every call is on the hottest path. `field` is `wholeValueField` for a value destination.
`applyString` takes every call of a string, the empty-span opening and closing calls included,
with `StringInfo` marking which (see `StreamStringConvertible`). There is no separate finish:
the call carrying `.end` is it.
