    switch element {
    case .valueStreamString: .arrayStreamString
    case .valueOptionalStreamString: .arrayOptionalStreamString
    case .valueBool: .arrayBool
    case .valueOptionalBool: .arrayOptionalBool
    case .valueDouble: .arrayDouble
    case .valueInt: .arrayInt
    case .valueOptionalDouble: .arrayOptionalDouble
    case .valueOptionalInt: .arrayOptionalInt
    case .simd2Double: .arraySIMD2Double
    case .simd3Double: .arraySIMD3Double
    case .simd4Double: .arraySIMD4Double
    case .optionalSIMD2Double: .arrayOptionalSIMD2Double
    case .optionalSIMD3Double: .arrayOptionalSIMD3Double
    case .optionalSIMD4Double: .arrayOptionalSIMD4Double
    default: .generic
    }
  }

StreamSchema.swift:canHold.comment:
Whether a container of `kind` can be written through a destination of this shape: a JSON object
reaches both an object and a dictionary, every other pairing is a type mismatch. Without it a
scalar destination absorbs any container that reaches it, because a scalar frame ignores keys
and applies every token to itself.

StreamSchema.swift:childIndex.comment:
The position of the container's schema in the entering schema's ``StreamSchema/children``,
or ``reentering``.

StreamSchema.swift:childSchemaBits.comment:
The object address of the schema `frame` names, which the sink stores as a borrowed frame's
schema: `children` and `enterFieldOwner` are the owners, so no reference is formed here.

StreamSchema.swift:children.comment:
The schemas the frames ``enterField`` returns name by position. Held here so each one
outlives every parse that enters this schema; see ``StreamFrame``.

StreamSchema.swift:closureLaneRoute.comment:
The lane route that stores through the schema's `applyNumber` rather than a typed lane store,
for a vector one optional deeper than the typed routes' storage types describe.

StreamSchema.swift:completedValue.comment:
A converted container borrows its source's normal schema while the sink remembers where
to write its completed value. Ordinary schemas carry nil; ordinary frames stay 24 bytes.

StreamSchema.swift:declaredFields.comment: The members the field table was built from, in declaration order; empty without a table.

StreamSchema.swift:elementKind.comment:
The child's `scalarKind` and `scalarOptional`, cached on the container so the frame over it
can copy them at push time: a scalar arriving at an array, dictionary or fixed-array frame
reads a byte off the frame rather than chasing the element schema.

StreamSchema.swift:elementOptional.code:
@inlinable
  static func elementOptional(_ bits: UInt32) -> Bool { bits & Self.elementOptionalBit != 0 }

StreamSchema.swift:elementSchema.comment:
The schema an array's elements or a dictionary's values are written through. Data on the
parent, not a value the closure returns: returning a `StreamFrame` meant a retain on the way
out and a release when the sink lowered it, per element. The bits are what the sink copies
into a frame (see `StreamFieldEntry.schemaBits`); the strong reference is the owner.

StreamSchema.swift:elementStride.comment:
For a fixed array whose elements sit at a stride from its storage -- an `InlineArray`, a SIMD
vector's lanes: the sink addresses element `i` at `storage + i * elementStride` and calls
nothing. Zero for every other schema.

StreamSchema.swift:enterField.comment:
Returns a frame for the container stored at `field`, materializing it when absent. It is not
reset when present, so a repeated key resumes the container the first occurrence built.
`ContainerReentryTests` pins that and the scalar cases, which do not agree with each other:
a repeated string concatenates and a repeated number replaces.

StreamSchema.swift:enterFieldOwner.comment:
The schema `StreamFrame.reentering` names: nil for this one, or the schema a wrapper forwards
`enterField` and `children` from. Not the wrapper itself, which writes differently -- an optional
wrapper materialises its storage first, and the frame's storage need not be an optional. Strong,
so the wrapper owns everything its frames can name.

StreamSchema.swift:enterKey.comment:
Returns the slot of the value stored under a dynamic key, written through
``elementSchema``. Dictionaries only.

StreamSchema.swift:fieldIndex.comment: The open-addressed index over `fields`, or nil below `StreamFieldTable.indexThreshold`.

StreamSchema.swift:fields.comment:
The field table (StreamFieldTable.swift), or nil for a schema that routes keys through
`matchField`. Every macro-generated object schema carries one. The owner is `fields`; the
sink reads the three raw views, because loading a class reference off a frame's
`unowned(unsafe)` schema is a retain and a release, and the sink does it per key.

StreamSchema.swift:fixedElementCount.comment:
Negative for a dynamic array. Kept off the frame: only an InlineArray's open and close need
it, while adding it to BorrowedFrame would grow every frame from 24 to 32 bytes.

StreamSchema.swift:ignoresKeys.comment:
Whether this schema declares no matcher. Read when one schema is wrapped in another, so the
wrapper does not install a matcher over a destination that has none.

StreamSchema.swift:init.code:
public convenience init(
    shape: Shape,
    prepareRoot: @escaping @Sendable (UnsafeMutableRawPointer) -> Void = { _ in },
    matchField: (@Sendable (Span<UInt8>) -> Int32)? = nil,
    onFieldRecognized: (@Sendable (UnsafeMutableRawPointer, StreamFieldID) -> Void)? = nil,
    applyString: @escaping @Sendable (
      UnsafeMutableRawPointer, Int32, Span<UInt8>, StringInfo
    ) -> StreamApplyResult = { _, _, _, _ in .unsupported },
    applyNumber: @escaping @Sendable (
      UnsafeMutableRawPointer, Int32, Span<UInt8>, NumberInfo
    ) -> StreamApplyResult = { _, _, _, _ in .unsupported },
    applyBoolean: @escaping @Sendable (
      UnsafeMutableRawPointer, Int32, Bool
    ) -> StreamApplyResult = { _, _, _ in .unsupported },
    applyNull: @escaping @Sendable (UnsafeMutableRawPointer, Int32) -> StreamApplyResult = {
      _, _ in .unsupported
    },
    enterField: @escaping @Sendable (UnsafeMutableRawPointer, Int32) -> StreamFrame? = { _, _ in nil },
    children: [StreamSchema] = [],
    appendElement: @escaping @Sendable (UnsafeMutableRawPointer, Int32) -> UnsafeMutableRawPointer? = {
      _, _ in nil
    },
    enterKey: @escaping @Sendable (UnsafeMutableRawPointer, Span<UInt8>) -> UnsafeMutableRawPointer? = {
      _, _ in nil
    },
    elementSchema: StreamSchema? = nil,
    fields: [StreamField] = []
  ) {
    self.init(
      shape: shape,
      prepareRoot: prepareRoot,
      matchField: matchField,
      onFieldRecognized: onFieldRecognized,
      applyString: applyString,
      applyNumber: applyNumber,
      applyBoolean: applyBoolean,
      applyNull: applyNull,
      enterField: enterField,
      children: children,
      appendElement: appendElement,
      enterKey: enterKey,
      elementSchema: elementSchema,
      leafRoute: .generic,
      fixedElementCount: -1,
      fields: fields.isEmpty ? nil : StreamFieldTable(fields)
    )
  }
StreamSchema.swift:init.comment:
Describes how the parser writes into a value of one shape.

A closure left out rejects its token kind: the default `applyString`, `applyNumber`,
`applyBoolean` and `applyNull` return ``StreamApplyResult/unsupported``, which the parser
reports as a type mismatch. `fields` is the declarative way to route an object's keys, and it
outranks `matchField` when both are given; a duplicate key in `fields` stops the program.
The closures take raw storage: `UnsafeMutableRawPointer` is the address of the value this
schema describes, and each must write only through the type it was built for. `enterField`
names the schema of each container it opens by its position in `children`; see
``StreamFrame``.

`matchField` is optional rather than defaulted so that "no matcher" is a fact the schema
carries rather than one indistinguishable from a matcher that happens to answer -1.

StreamSchema.swift:keyDispatch.comment: Only key recognition consults hooks; scalar/container routing retains its original flag.

StreamSchema.swift:leafRoute.comment:
Bit casts, not `init(rawValue:)`: the word was packed from these enums, and the raw-value
initialiser is a range check and an unwrap on every read, which put a dozen instructions
back into each scalar entry point.

Exact homogeneous operations the sink may perform without constructing a StreamFrame or
calling a stored closure. Hand-written schemas and unrecognized protocol conformers remain
`.generic`, preserving the public API's open-ended behavior.

StreamSchema.swift:matchField.comment: Returns the field identifier for a key, or -1 when the destination has no such field.

StreamSchema.swift:onFieldRecognized.comment:
Called once for each recognized object key, before its value is applied.
Aliases share an identifier; unknown keys are not reported. Nil incurs no hook dispatch.

StreamSchema.swift:pendingField.comment: The field whose value is pending, or `-1`. Leave the default for a new frame.

StreamSchema.swift:prepareRoot.comment:
Prepares root storage before a container frame begins writing through this schema.

Most roots already hold their initialized value and need no work. Wrappers such as
`Optional` use this hook to materialize storage even when an empty container produces no
field or element events that would otherwise do so.

StreamSchema.swift:reentering.comment:
The ``childIndex`` that names the schema whose ``StreamSchema/enterField`` returned the frame.

A schema cannot list itself among its own children, so a self-similar container -- a node
whose `child` member is another node -- names its schema this way.

StreamSchema.swift:routeBits.comment:
`leafRoute`, `elementKind` and `elementOptional` in one word, which is what a frame copies at
push and the sink caches as its active route: one load and one store, where three bytes
measured as a 1-3% drift on every corpus. Layout in `StreamRouteBits`.

StreamSchema.swift:scalarKind.comment:
The kind of value this schema writes when it stands over a scalar, in the same vocabulary the
field table uses for an object's members, so an array element, dictionary value or SIMD lane of
a known type is a typed store at the slot rather than a closure call. `custom` for anything
else; `scalarOptional` says the slot is an `Optional` opened `.some`, so a null writes `nil`.

StreamSchema.swift:storage.comment: The address of the container being written. It must stay valid until the container closes.

StreamSchema.swift:streamArrayElementSch.comment:
The schema this type is written through as an array element, and the value the array opens
the element's slot with. ``StreamSchema/Usage/arrayElement``.

These differ from ``streamSchema`` and ``StreamInitializable/streamInitialValue()`` only for
`Optional`: an array owns the slot it hands out and can open it already materialised, so an
optional element never checks for `nil` before a write, where a bare optional *root* must.
Worth 2.4x on `[Int?]` (PROGRESSION.md, "The optional seam"). The defaults are the root
forms, so every type but `Optional` conforms without saying anything.

StreamSchema.swift:streamArrayElementSch.code:
@inlinable
  public static var streamArrayElementSchema: StreamSchema { Self.streamSchema }

StreamSchema.swift:streamDictionaryValue.comment:
The schema this type is written through as a dictionary value, and the value the dictionary
opens the value's slot with. ``StreamSchema/Usage/dictionaryValue``.

A dictionary owns the slot it opens under a key exactly as an array owns an element's, so
the defaults are the array-element forms, which is what `Optional` relies on.

StreamSchema.swift:streamDictionaryValue.code:
@inlinable
  public static var streamDictionaryValueSchema: StreamSchema { Self.streamArrayElementSchema }

StreamSchema.swift:streamInitialArrayEle.code:
@inlinable
  public static func streamInitialArrayElement() -> Self { Self.streamInitialValue() }

StreamSchema.swift:streamInitialDictiona.code:
@inlinable
  public static func streamInitialDictionaryValue() -> Self { Self.streamInitialArrayElement() }

StreamSchema.swift:streamObjectMemberSch.comment:
The schema a container entry installs on the frame it pushes when this type is a declared
member of an object. ``StreamSchema/Usage/objectMember``.

Separated from the frame so a caller can resolve it once and store it: `streamSchema` is a
computed property on every generic partial, so reading it per entry allocates per container
occurrence and leaves the entry's frame as the schema's only owner. The macro resolves it
once per schema build, and the parent's field table owns the result.

StreamSchema.swift:streamObservationFiel.comment:
Direct stored key paths used to validate field observation. Generated by `@StreamParseable`.

Custom roots must list every stored member, including members ignored by their schema,
so observation can reject ambiguous overlapping storage. Do not include computed or
nested paths. The default empty list disables field observation.

StreamSchema.swift:streamView.comment:
Builds a view over a value at `storage`.

The lifetime dependency on `storage` ties the returned view's borrow-checked scope to the
call site: the pointer itself carries no lifetime of its own, but the dependency still
forces callers through an API shape (like a `withView`-style closure) that cannot let the
view outlive the call that produced it.

A correct snapshot without a recursive rebuild: every container the parser writes into holds
its open element in an inline slot, so a copy shares only storage that is sealed and never
written again, and the open element's own buffers copy on write at the next append.

StreamSchema.swift:templateOwner.comment:
The box owning the element template a container schema's `appendElement`/`enterKey` copies
from, or nil for a schema with no template. Held only to bound the template's lifetime by the
schema's: the closures capture the raw pointer, never this. See `_StreamTemplateStorage`.

StreamSchema.swift:wholeValueField.comment:
The field an apply closure receives when the destination *is* the value rather than a field
of one -- an array element, a dictionary value, a bare scalar root.

Must stay negative so it cannot collide with a declared field: at zero it collided with the
first member a generated object schema declares, and an object schema's `default:
.unsupported` is what turns those back into the mismatches they are.

StreamSchemaBuilders.swift:_streamApply.comment: Partial members are optional, so a value has to exist before it can be appended to.
The capacity is a first-chunk hint for a `StreamString` member; a nested one goes without it.

StreamSchemaBuilders.swift:_streamApplyT.comment:
A member two optionals deep: the partial is `T??`, one layer past what the overloads above
unwrap, so without these it fell to the disfavoured catch-alls and every value was a mismatch.
The pattern only matches a double optional, so no `T?` member resolves differently. The slow path
on purpose: it applies through `Optional<T>`'s root schema, which materialises before it writes,
at the inner optional's address -- the offset-zero payload the frame entry helpers rely on.

StreamSchemaBuilders.swift:_streamFieldR.comment:
What a member's type resolves to for the field table, by `_streamApply`'s overload structure, so
classification matches application. Two overloads per protocol (optional and initialised
modes), all taking the hoisted container schema so the macro emits one call shape. The
`prepare` closures capture nothing; the capacity arrives from the entry.

No built-in container spelling: resolve through the actual partial storage type, which covers
aliases, generic spelling and user-defined containers.
A type none of the protocols describe stays on the closures.

Capacity-aware forms are container-specific: each container maps the hint onto its own storage.
The capacity travels on the entry, so the closure has no context.

A `String` member has no table kind, so the hint rides on its apply closure instead (see
`_streamApply(_:utf8:initialCapacity:)`); the route only has to stay `.custom`.

Overload resolution sees through aliases the macro cannot: an alias of a `StreamArray` or
`StreamDictionary` partial selects a concrete overload above. These fallbacks keep an annotation
on a scalar or object from silently becoming a no-op.

StreamSchemaBuilders.swift:_streamObject.comment:
The schema a field's container entry installs, or nil for non-container storage. The macro
calls this once per field per schema build, and the field table owns the result, so it outlives
every frame that borrows it; reading `T.streamSchema` in the entry allocated one per container
occurrence. The overload
pair mirrors `_streamEnterField`'s, so nil here means the entry answers nil too.

StreamSchemaBuilders.swift:_streamSchema.comment:
A fixed-width SIMD value is syntactically a generic type but semantically an array-shaped
container.

Delegates to the core's scalar constructors, which root conformances also use, so a type cannot
be described one way as a field and another as a root.

An element one optional deeper than the optional container builders unwrap: the macro peels a
single layer, so `[T??]` reaches here with `Optional<T>`. None of the typed overloads above take
an `Optional`, so no member that type-checked before resolves differently. The optional root
schema materialises before each write, which is the correct path for the deeper layer.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:Entry.comment:
One type's schema for one usage in a ``StreamSchemaCache``, and the closure that builds it.

Made by ``StreamSchemaCache/entry(for:usage:build:)``, for a concrete type to keep in a
`static let`: reading through it costs a lock round trip, where a read by type also hashes.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:_streamSchemaCac.comment:
Guards every cache's entries and every entry's schema. Held only to read or swap a reference;
builds run outside it.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:build.comment: Nil only for an entry a read by type made, which is never handed out.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:cached.comment: Guarded by `lock`, so unchecked for the reason `entries` is.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:contains.comment: Whether a schema is cached for `type` in `usage`.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:entries.comment:
Guarded by `lock`. An entry handed out is never removed, only emptied: a `static let` may
hold it, and a second entry for the same key would cache beside it, unseen by `count` and
`removeAll()`. One a read by type made, which has no build of its own and is never handed
out, is replaced when `entry(for:usage:build:)` supplies one.
Unchecked because the lock already serialises every access: the dynamic check was a
`swift_beginAccess`/`swift_endAccess` pair per read, ~40 ns on `StreamArray<Int>`.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:entry.comment:
The entry holding `type`'s schema for `usage`, built by `build`, for a concrete type to keep
in a `static let`.

The entry owns its build, so every read of it -- and every read of the key by type -- builds
the same way, on first read and again after removal. The first closure supplied for a key is
the one kept; a later call returns the same entry and drops its own. `build` follows the
contract of ``schema(for:usage:build:)``, and must be `@Sendable` because the entry keeps it
and any thread may run it.

Reading through the entry skips the lookup by type; the entry is still this cache's, so
``count``, ``contains(_:usage:)`` and removal see what it holds.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:lock.comment: `_streamSchemaCacheLock`, held so a read does not call `swift_once` to reach the global.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:published.comment: Published once and never released: removal does nothing on Embedded.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:removeAll.comment: Removes every cached schema. Streams already running keep theirs.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:removeSchema.comment:
Removes the schema cached for `type` in `usage`, returning it.

A stream already running keeps its schemas; the next read builds a fresh one.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:schema.comment:
The schema cached for `type` in `usage`, building and storing it if there is none.

A miss builds with the entry's own closure when ``entry(for:usage:build:)`` supplied one, so
every read of a key builds the same way, and with `build` otherwise. It runs outside the
cache's lock, because a schema build reads its members' schemas,
which may be cached here too. Two threads that miss at once both build, and the first to
finish is the one every caller gets. So `build` may run more than once -- and on Embedded
Swift it runs on every call -- and must have no side effects. It must not read the schema
it is building.

Only the lookup is out of line: `build` is formed at the call site, where its generic
parameters are concrete, so the schema it builds is specialised.

A hit touches only the schema: handing the entry out too cost a retain and release, 50 ns a
read on `StreamArray<Int>`. A miss prefers the entry's own build.
The schema, built by the entry's own closure on the first read and after removal.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:shared.comment: The process-wide cache, used by `@StreamParseable` and the library's own conformances.

StreamSchemaCache.swift:store.comment: The first schema stored wins; a racing build's is dropped.

StreamString+Reading.swift:StreamString.comment:
Forward `Character` access. Grapheme segmentation is not public API, so boundaries come from
`String`'s own breaker over a small decoded window, grown while its first character fills it.

Byte-wise, and named for it: each borrows the foreign text's UTF-8 once and hands it to
`utf8Matches`, which walks the storage windows.

StreamString+Reading.swift:scalarIndex.comment:
The scalar-view index before `index`.

Walks back over at most three continuation bytes. When the lead byte reached does not span
back to `index`, the byte before `index` stands alone as U+FFFD, so backward and forward
traversal visit the same positions.

StreamString+Reading.swift:streamASCIITa.comment:
The order of two texts whose bytes agree up to an offset and are ASCII from there, given each
one's byte at that offset, `nil` where it has ended: negative, zero or positive.

StreamString+Reading.swift:streamLastByt.comment:
Whether two texts are unequal by their last bytes alone, each `nil` when its text is empty.

An ASCII last byte is the last scalar of the normalized text as well: nothing composes with it
or reorders past it, and it ends any sequence left open before it. Two that differ settle `==`
without reading further, as does an empty text against one that is not, since no text
normalizes to nothing. That is the comparison a deduplicated stream makes, a value against its
own snapshot from one append earlier, so it stays O(1) rather than a scan of both.

StreamString+Reading.swift:textEquals.comment: Whether the text equals `other` as `String` compares them.

StreamString+Reading.swift:utf8LastByte.comment: The last accumulated byte, or `nil` when there is none.

StreamString+Reading.swift:utf8Ordering.comment:
`String`'s order for the text against the UTF-8 in `buffer` when the bytes decide it, or
`nil` when a non-ASCII byte follows their first difference and only decoding can.

StreamString+Reading.swift:utf8Search.comment:
A first-byte scan with a full match at each candidate, so the worst case is quadratic. The
caller range-checks `offset`, so its `precondition` names its own type.

StreamString.swift:==.comment: Free functions: a member operator must take `StreamString` itself somewhere.

StreamString.swift:CharacterSequence.comment:
The accumulated text as the same forward sequence of extended grapheme clusters that a
Swift `String` exposes as `Character` elements.

StreamString.swift:StreamString.comment:
String storage a parser appends raw UTF-8 to, decoding once when it is read.

This is what a `String` member of a `@StreamParseable` type is stored as in its `Partial`.
Appending a chunk copies bytes and never builds a `String`, and a snapshot shares every block the
parser has finished with, so reading the value after every chunk stays cheap. Convert with
`String(_:)` to read the text.

**Comparison follows `String`.** `==`, `<` and `hash(into:)`, and `==` against a `String` or
any `StringProtocol`, use canonical equivalence, so two spellings of one character are equal.
Most comparisons never decode: the bytes are compared first, and both sides are decoded and
compared as `String`s only when a non-ASCII byte follows the first byte where they differ.
Different lengths alone do not make two values unequal. `==` settles most unequal pairs from
their last bytes, such as a value against its snapshot from before an append, and otherwise
reads both values up to their first difference.

**Searching is by UTF-8 bytes**, and the names say so: ``hasUTF8Prefix(_:)``,
``hasUTF8Suffix(_:)``, ``containsUTF8(_:)``, ``utf8Range(of:from:)`` and ``isUTF8Prefix(of:)``
compare bytes, which for decoded JSON text is scalar by scalar, and never normalize:

```swift
StreamString("\u{E9}") == StreamString("e\u{301}")      // true, as for `String`
StreamString("e\u{301}").hasUTF8Prefix("\u{E9}")         // false: the bytes differ
StreamString("e\u{301}").containsUTF8("e")               // true: scalar, not grapheme, aligned
```

Convert to `String` first to search by canonical equivalence.

The read side of `Span<UInt8>._streamPaddedWord(at:)`'s encoding, so a generated `String`-raw
enum matcher compares a value against a literal with the same codegen it uses for object keys,
and never materializes a `String`.
The primitives the read layer in `StreamString+Reading.swift` is written against.

As `String` compares: canonical equivalence, decoding only when a non-ASCII byte follows the
first difference. See `StreamString+Reading.swift`.

Against `String` directly, because `partial.title == expected` is the commonest client
comparison. Canonical equivalence like `==`; the optional overloads exist because optional
lifting only reaches the homogeneous operator.
Byte-wise, unlike `==`, and named for it: the scalar-exact answer with no decode.

Hashes what `==` compares, the normalized text. ASCII is its own normalization, so it hashes in
place; anything else is normalized through `String`. Both feed the bytes and then 0xFF, which no
UTF-8 contains, and `Hasher` sees one byte stream however it is split, so the two paths agree on
equal text: `"K"` and the Kelvin sign `"\u{212A}"` are equal, and only one of them is ASCII.

As `String` orders: by normalized scalars, which the bytes decide unless a non-ASCII byte follows
the first difference. See `StreamString+Reading.swift`.

`@unchecked` because a `ManagedBuffer` subclass cannot be `Sendable`; the chunks are written only
while uniquely held, the grounds `StreamArray` asserts it on.
Otherwise a reflecting printer dumps the blocks and the tail.
A single value, encoding as the string it stands in for. Outside the Embedded subset.

StreamString.swift:StreamStringChunkHead.comment: A `StreamString` block: one allocation for a header and the bytes, as `StreamBlock`.

StreamString.swift:StringInterpolation.comment: Custom, so segments append as bytes instead of assembling a `String` first.

StreamString.swift:Substring.comment:
`StreamString` cannot conform to `StringProtocol` (it requires `String.Index` positions and
`Character` elements, and the stdlib admits only `String` and `Substring`), so this bridges:
one decode, then the full `String` API.

StreamString.swift:UTF8View.comment:
A random access view of the accumulated UTF-8 bytes.

Byte offsets are the currency for substrings: a renderer that has drawn the first `n` bytes
asks for `string.utf8[n...]` and decodes just the suffix, without materializing what it
already drew.

StreamString.swift:UnicodeScalarView.comment:
A bidirectional view of the accumulated bytes as Unicode scalars.

Indices are byte offsets, the same currency as ``utf8``, so an index moves freely between
the two views. Ill-formed bytes decode as the repairing `String` decode does: one U+FFFD per
byte that cannot begin a sequence, and one per sequence cut short. Table-free, so it stays
inside the embedded subset.

StreamString.swift:_streamPaddedLeadingW.comment:
The first eight accumulated UTF-8 bytes as one little-endian word.

- SeeAlso: ``_streamPaddedWord(at:)``

StreamString.swift:_streamPaddedWord.comment:
The accumulated UTF-8 bytes `start..<start + 8`, little-endian, zero-padded past
``utf8Count``.

A matcher must still test ``utf8Count``: a value may hold a decoded NUL, which the padding is
otherwise indistinguishable from. `start` must be a multiple of eight, so the word never
crosses a 512-byte block.

StreamString.swift:append.comment:
Appends another accumulation, one contiguous storage window at a time, without materializing
either side.
Appends a single character's UTF-8 bytes.

StreamString.swift:appendInterpolation.comment: `String(describing:)` is reflection, outside the Embedded subset.

StreamString.swift:appendWhole.comment:
A whole string in one call -- `PartialSink.writeTableString`, the table's string member -- as
`append(utf8:)` does it, with neither copy a `memmove` call. A short value takes the overlapping
word copy (the call, through its stub and `memmove`'s size and overlap dispatch, cost more than
the copy); a long one, landing on an empty value, takes one exact allocation and one copy in
`promoteWholeInlineStorage`.

A separate entry rather than a change to `append(utf8:)`, which the chunk path inlines all the
way into `JSONParser.parse`: there a byte-fed chunk's constant length of one folds the
`memmove` to a single `strb`, and either an outlined or an inlined ladder in its place cost
typed LLM byte by byte 7-11% (outlined, a call per byte; inlined, `appendBlocked` stopped
inlining into `parse`).

StreamString.swift:blockShift.comment:
512 bytes: the unhinted first block and the canonical logical window. The 8 KiB cap bounds the
tail a snapshot can force an append to copy; a hint may start the schedule anywhere in range.

StreamString.swift:blocks.comment:
The tail's: the sealed blocks ahead of it, in order. Moved out when the tail seals, so a sealed
block holds none and no block reaches itself.

StreamString.swift:byteCapacity.comment: Not `capacity`: `ManagedBuffer` owns that name for its `malloc_size` read.

StreamString.swift:capacity.comment: Stored rather than read back from `malloc_size` the way `ManagedBuffer.capacity` does.

StreamString.swift:characters.comment: The accumulated text as forward `Character` values, agreeing with iteration over `String`.

StreamString.swift:containsUTF8.comment: Whether `other`'s UTF-8 occurs anywhere in the accumulated bytes, compared byte-wise.

StreamString.swift:copyBytes.comment: One memcpy inline; blocked, one per block touched plus one for the tail.

StreamString.swift:count.comment: The bytes written. The owning value makes the chunk unique before changing anything here.

StreamString.swift:decode.comment:
Decodes `range`, repairing rather than validating: a repairing decode cannot fail, which is
what lets this be a plain `String` read rather than a throwing one.

StreamString.swift:decodeScalar.comment:
Decodes the scalar at `position`, repairing as the `String` decode does: a byte that cannot
begin a sequence is U+FFFD of length one, and a sequence cut short is one U+FFFD over its
maximal subpart. The narrowed second-byte ranges reject overlong forms and surrogates.

StreamString.swift:hasUTF8Prefix.comment: Whether the accumulated bytes start with `prefix`'s UTF-8, compared byte-wise.

StreamString.swift:hasUTF8Suffix.comment: Whether the accumulated bytes end with `suffix`'s UTF-8, compared byte-wise.

StreamString.swift:init.comment:
Every property's value is its declared default. Measured: assigning the three here instead
built the value on the stack and copied it, an outlined retain and release of the `nil` tail
on every member opened, because the optimizer does not forward the stores of a struct this
many fields wide.
Decodes the accumulated bytes, repairing any ill-formed UTF-8.

Decodes a byte range of a ``StreamString``, repairing any ill-formed UTF-8.

A slice's bounds are byte offsets, so a boundary that lands inside a multi-byte character
decodes with replacement characters at the cut. Offsets that came from the view itself —
a previously read `endIndex`, a delta boundary — land between characters and decode clean.
Decodes the accumulated bytes into a `Substring`, repairing any ill-formed UTF-8.

Decodes a byte range of a ``StreamString`` into a `Substring`, repairing any ill-formed
UTF-8.

StreamString.swift:inlineBytes.comment: Held in the value: a copied short string needs no refcount, a short append no allocation.

StreamString.swift:isUTF8Prefix.comment:
Whether the accumulated bytes are a prefix of `text`'s UTF-8, compared byte-wise —
including when they are all of it.

The direction a *streaming* match needs: whether what has arrived so far is still consistent
with `text`. A generated enum matcher walks its cases shortest-first asking this, so the
first case still consistent with the bytes in hand is the shortest one.

StreamString.swift:promoteSizedInlineSto.comment:
The first overflow append sizes the schedule from the *whole* byte count in hand (a reservation
uses half), so one big span lands in one block. Never lowers a reserved shift. Measured: LLM
bulk +73.7%, GSoC +11.6%; `@inline(never)` because inlined into every `stringChunk` site it
flips the parse loop's inlining. See PROGRESSION.md.

StreamString.swift:promoteWholeInlineSto.comment:
`promoteSizedInlineStorage` followed by the append, for `appendWhole`. A value still empty
whose bytes fit its first block without filling it -- nearly every whole string past the
inline form -- is one exact allocation and one copy, skipping `appendBlocked`'s uniqueness
call and loop over a chunk made a moment ago; that leaves the state `appendBlocked` would.

StreamString.swift:reallocateTail.comment:
Copies the tail into a chunk of `capacity`: a snapshot shares it, or it is too small. A unique
tail hands its sealed blocks over; a shared one keeps them for the value it is shared with.

StreamString.swift:scalarAlignedOffset.comment:
The largest scalar-aligned offset at or before `limit`, backing off over at most three
continuation bytes, so a window cut never tears a scalar.

StreamString.swift:sealTail.comment:
The full tail joins the sealed blocks and a `nextCapacity` block takes its place, allocated now
because a promoted value always has a tail; only a value ending exactly on a seal wastes it.
The tail is unique here: the append that filled it made it so.

StreamString.swift:sealedPosition.comment:
Inverts `sealedPrefix`: inside the doubling ramp the block is `log2((position >> s) + 1)`, one
`clz`; past it, a shift and a mask.

StreamString.swift:sealedPrefix.comment:
Bytes sealed ahead of block `k`: while the schedule doubles, prefix sums are the geometric
series `2^(s+k) - 2^s`; past the cap they grow linearly at `2^13` per block.

StreamString.swift:setStartBlockShift.comment:
(Re)starts the schedule and the tail cache at `shift`. Only called while the bytes are inline,
which keeps both consistent with no sealed blocks.

StreamString.swift:startBlockShift.comment: The first sealed block's shift; block `k` uses `min(startBlockShift + k, maximumBlockShift)`.

StreamString.swift:storageBits.comment:
Low byte: the inline count (0...64). Bits 8..15: the first block's shift (block `k` holds
`1 << min(shift + k, 13)` bytes). Bits 16..23: the tail block's shift, `min(first +
blocks.count, 13)`, cached so the append path reads a word it already loads. Measured: reading
`blocks.count` instead cost -6..-17% on the byte-fed rows.

StreamString.swift:streamCopyShortBytes.comment:
Copies `count` bytes, 0...64, between two non-overlapping ranges without a `memmove` call:
overlapping 16-byte moves from both ends at 16...64 (two pairs past 32), and an 8/4/2/1 ladder
below. Every load stays inside `[source, source + count)` -- a span is exact, so nothing past its
end is known to be readable -- and every store inside `[destination, destination + count)`.
Each size class loads before it stores.

StreamString.swift:streamInitialValue.code: public static func streamInitialValue() -> Self { Self() }

StreamString.swift:streamReserve.comment:
Reserves room for `utf8ByteCount` UTF-8 bytes, promoting out of the inline representation
when the request cannot fit there.

A request that is not larger than the current count, negative ones included, does nothing.

StreamString.swift:tail.comment:
`nil` while the bytes are inline, so opening a short value is a zeroed write and dropping it a
null release. Past that, the filling block, the only allocated storage an append touches and so
the most it can copy; its header holds the sealed blocks, which are never written again and
follow the schedule, see `sealedPosition(of:)`. One reference however many blocks: a copy is
one retain, and the inline test is this word.

StreamString.swift:tailBlockCapacity.comment: The capacity of the block the tail is currently filling, read from the cached shift.

StreamString.swift:tailChunk.comment: The rest are for a promoted value only.

StreamString.swift:unicodeScalars.comment: The accumulated bytes as Unicode scalars, indexed by byte offset.

StreamString.swift:usesInlineStorage.comment:
`@inlinable` because `append(utf8:)` and `utf8Count` are: out of line, a client specialisation
copied the whole value to the stack and called out per append. One-way: a value that has left
inline storage keeps a tail, empty or not.

StreamString.swift:utf8.comment: The accumulated bytes as a random access collection.

StreamString.swift:utf8Byte.comment: The byte read every view routes through.

StreamString.swift:utf8CommonPrefixCount.comment: One `streamFirstDifference` per 512-byte window, which both values cut at the same offsets.

StreamString.swift:utf8Count.comment: The number of UTF-8 bytes accumulated so far.

StreamString.swift:utf8Matches.comment:
Whether `buffer` matches the bytes at `offset`: one `streamBytesEqual` per window touched.
Shared by the searchers, which are byte-wise.

StreamString.swift:utf8Ordering.comment:
`String`'s order for two values when their bytes decide it, or `nil` when only decoding can.
`common` is their common prefix's length when the caller already has it.

StreamString.swift:utf8Range.comment:
The byte range of the first occurrence of `needle`'s UTF-8 at or after `offset`, compared
byte-wise.

The bounds are byte offsets. A match in well-formed text is scalar-aligned but not
necessarily grapheme-aligned: `"e"` matches inside a decomposed `"é"`. An empty needle matches
emptily at `offset`. The worst case is quadratic.

StreamString.swift:withWindow.comment:
Runs `body` over `[position, position + count)`, which must not cross a 512-byte window: seals
and the tail are 512-aligned after promotion, and an inline value is one window.

StreamString.swift:write.comment: Block-at-a-time, each cut backed off to a scalar boundary; never materializes the whole value.

StreamTemplateStorage.swift:_StreamField.comment:
One field table entry's ``StreamFieldPrepare``, held as a `let` so the sink can call it through
a guaranteed reference.

The table stores the box's address, retained once, rather than the closure: a closure loaded
out of pointer memory is a copy, so every container member open retained and released its
context, and since the memory was typed by a generic `Pointee` the closure was stored at maximal
abstraction, so the call also went through a reabstraction thunk with both arguments spilled.
The same pair `_withUnsafeGuaranteedRef` removed from the schema's own closures (PROGRESSION.md,
"The last closure pairs").

StreamTemplateStorage.swift:_StreamTempl.comment: Test-only: `StreamSchemaLifetimeTests` asserts repeated streams do not grow the live count.

Owns a template value for the lifetime of the schema that copies elements from it.

Handed to the schema's closures as a bare `UnsafePointer`: a captured class reference would be
a load and, in some closure shapes, a retain/release per element. The schema outlives every
parse that borrows it (`PartialSink` holds schemas `unowned(unsafe)`).

StreamTemplateStorage.swift:_streamOwned.comment:
Allocates a template value at a stable address, owned by the returned box.

Built once here rather than in the element closure: a generic element's `Self()` re-enters the
runtime's locking metadata cache per open, and returning it by value is a second whole-element
copy.

StreamTemplateStorage.swift:_streamTempl.comment: Templates currently allocated, and templates allocated since process start. Debug only.

StreamTemplateStorage.swift:address.comment: The template, typed. The builders bind this to a local and capture *that*, never `self`.

StreamTemplateStorage.swift:destroy.comment: Type-erased destroy and deallocate: a closure rather than a generic parameter on the class.

StreamTemplateStorage.swift:value.code: var value: (live: Int, total: Int) { self.counts.withLock { $0 } }

StreamUTF8Match.swift:StreamUTF8Match.comment:
A byte-exact match against the UTF-8 encoding of a string.

The generated predicates expect an expression whose value provides `count`,
`_streamPaddedLeadingWord()`, and `_streamPaddedWord(at:)`, such as `Span<UInt8>`.

StreamUTF8Match.swift:StreamUTF8MatchSet.comment: A byte-exact predicate that accepts any of several UTF-8 strings.

StreamUTF8Match.swift:condition.comment:
Generates a complete byte-exact equality predicate.

The expression may occur more than once in the returned syntax. Bind
side-effecting input to a local first when it must be evaluated exactly once.

Generates a predicate that is true when any value matches.

An empty set produces `false`. The input expression may occur more than once.

StreamUTF8Match.swift:init.comment: Creates a set of accepted UTF-8 strings.

StreamUTF8Match.swift:value.comment: The string whose UTF-8 encoding is matched.

StreamUTF8Match.swift:values.comment: The accepted strings, in their original order.

StreamUTF8Validation.swift:streamHasAVX2.comment:
A lazily initialised global: every read is a once-token compare, then a load (x86_64
disassembly). Read it only behind `@inline(never)`, as here -- in an inlined scan loop the
accessor cost CITM -9.9% (PROGRESSION.md).

Whether the 64-byte block classifiers (AVX2.c) may be called: AVX2 plus PCLMULQDQ and POPCNT.
Read once per parser, into `JSONParser.blockKernelsAvailable`, and never on a parse path.

StreamUTF8Validation.swift:streamValidat.comment:
The validator the parser calls: table lookups and overlapping loads where the platform has
them (see `StreamParsingShims.h`, where lane shifting in the run loop was measured 10% slower
and dropped; only a block with nothing before it is shifted in, from zero).
Out of line by name for the tests; the parser inlines `streamValidateUTF8Inline` into its own
out-of-line `validateNonASCIIRun` instead, so a valid run costs one call, not two.
The compare-based path by name, so tests hold both paths to one oracle where the lookup exists.

SupportMacros.swift:SupportActivityMacro.comment:
A downstream enum macro using what `@StreamParseable` cannot spell: a converted associated
value, a custom payload name, and partial hooks.

SupportMacros.swift:SupportModelMacro.comment:
A downstream macro that also makes the whole type `StreamParseable`.

`total` is internal on a public type, so this host knows `streamPartialValue` cannot be
inlined and says so; the plan itself only sees the partial's access.

SupportMacros.swift:SupportPartialMacro.comment: A downstream macro supplies its own field model and adds its own view API.

SupportMacros.swift:providingMacros.code:
let providingMacros: [Macro.Type] = [
    SupportPartialMacro.self, SupportFullPartialMacro.self, SupportMatcherMacro.self,

SwiftCollections.swift:Deque.comment:
Destinations to convert into, not members to parse into: only `[T]` and `[String: T]` route as
containers, and none of these is `StreamParseable`, so declaring one as a member of a parseable
type is a compile error rather than a value that silently stays empty.

SwiftCollections.swift:OrderedDictionary.comment: StreamDictionary keeps insertion order, so this conversion is lossless in both directions.

SwiftCollections.swift:TreeDictionary.comment: Order is not preserved here, because TreeDictionary does not have one.

SyntaxUtilities.swift:streamDeclarationS.comment: `signature { body }`, with `body` on its own lines one level in.

SyntaxUtilities.swift:streamIndented.comment: Indents every non-empty line of `text` by `spaces`.

SyntaxUtilities.swift:streamIsOptional.comment: Whether the type has a syntactically explicit optional layer.

SyntaxUtilities.swift:streamUnwrappedOpt.comment:
Removes one explicit optional layer (`T?`, `Optional<T>`, or `Swift.Optional<T>`), the layer
a partial member flattens: `T?` has the partial `T.Partial?`, so `T??` has
`Optional<T>.Partial?`. What remains is spelled `Optional<T>` rather than `T?`, so that
`.Partial` can follow it. Does not resolve type aliases or unwrap optional elements inside
containers.

One layer, not every layer: stripping them all described a `T??` member's storage as `T?`, and
the schemas built for that shape read and wrote the deeper storage as the shallower type.

SyntaxUtilities.swift:streamWordCaseLabe.comment:
The arm label matching exactly `key` in a `switch` over `input._streamPaddedLeadingWord()`,
where `byteCount` is `input`'s length.

Tagged.swift:Tagged.comment: Everything forwards to the raw value, so a tagged identifier accepts what its raw value does.
One stored property, so the raw value's schema applies to a pointer to the Tagged.

Explicit: a conditional conformance to a refined protocol (`StreamParseableObject`) does not
imply one to what it refines.
The schema comes from the root conformance above; this makes a tagged object a nested field.

Tagged.swift:init.comment: Structure preserving in both directions, so both conversions are the raw value's, rewrapped.

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_bmp_r.comment:
`stream_parsing_unescape_four_bmp` from the escape at `s + q`, written from `e`, for as long as
it holds and the run starts at or before `reach`, then two more if they are there; returns where
the run stopped.

Out of line, entered once per run. Two inline forms measured worse end to end: with literal
constants LLVM kept all fourteen in vector registers across the block loop, eight of them
callee-saved and saved on every kernel entry; with the constants behind a pointer made opaque
by an empty `asm`, the block loop was spill-free and the kernel alone as fast, yet raw
`Twitter escaped` gained +6.2% over the per-escape walk where this form gains +20.8%.

The first test turns away an escape whose digits, or the next one's, begin with `0` or `d`
(below U+1000, or U+D000 up and the surrogates): text whose escapes are mixed -- two-byte
scalars, surrogate pairs, `Fast Unicode escaped string` -- otherwise paid for the shape check
at every escape and decoded none of them (the kernel alone on that document: 4.9 us before
any of this, 13.6 with the check unguarded, 8.8 with this test; what is left is the call and
the pair taken as two escapes). It is here and not at the call: in the walk, the
two more loads and compares cost `LLM message` 3% end to end, through a register the block
loop then spilled.

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_first.comment: The lowest set bit's index, 64 for none (`rbit` + `clz`, which answers 64 for zero by itself).

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_four_.comment:
Four `\uXXXX` escapes in a row, each a three-byte scalar that is not a surrogate (U+0800 to
U+D7FF, U+E000 to U+FFFF), decoded together from the 24 bytes at `escape` (32 are read): their
12 bytes of UTF-8 in the low lanes of `*utf8`, junk in the top four. 0 when the 24 bytes are
anything else, and then nothing is concluded -- the scalar decode takes the escape as before.

Text in a script outside Latin serialised ASCII-only (Python's `json.dumps` default; all of
`twitterescaped`, 31,770 of whose 31,818 `\u` escapes are three-byte scalars, 85% of them in
runs of eight or more) is runs of exactly these. Three-byte scalars alone make the encoding a
fixed shuffle: escape i's digits n0..n3 sit at 6i + 2 .. 6i + 5 and its UTF-8 is
  0xE0 | n0,   0x80 | n1 << 2 | n2 >> 2,   0x80 | (n2 & 3) << 4 | n3,
so two `tbl` gathers (each byte's two digit sources) and two per-lane shifts make all twelve.
`two` (a constant at each call) asks the same of the first two escapes only, the first 12 bytes
and 6 of UTF-8: a run's remainder, which otherwise went one escape at a time through the scalar
decode (the kernel alone on `twitterescaped`: 69.0-70.7 -> 62.9-65.8 us).

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_hex_q.comment: Four hex digits as a UTF-16 code unit, or a value past 0xFFFF when one of them is not a digit.

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_recop.comment:
What follows an escape's selector, copied again one byte to the left of where the block store
put it. Sixty-four bytes however many are left in the block: two `ldp`/`stp` pairs against a
variable-length copy, and the slack the loop bound reserves is for exactly this.

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_run_l.comment:
Whether a `\u` escape's first digit is one a run of three-byte scalars mostly begins with:
anything but `0` and `d`/`D`. A filter only; the run's own check is the exact one.

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_start.comment:
Which backslashes of a block begin an escape, and through `escaped` which bytes are a selector
(the byte after such a backslash, itself a backslash or not). `next_is_escaped` carries "the
block before ended on an escape's backslash" in and out. This is simdjson's newer escape
scanner, not `stream_parsing_find_escaped`: that one marks only the byte after an odd-length run,
which is the question a quote asks, and says nothing of the backslashes inside the run.

A backslash not already a selector may begin an escape. Subtracting those from the odd bits
(with their successors set) carries through each run, leaving a pattern whose XOR with the odd
bits marks every second position of a run from its own start: the selectors, and one past an
odd run's end.

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_unico.comment:
The scalar a `\uXXXX` escape at `escape` (block offset `p`, the block's escape starts `starts`)
spells and, through `taken`, how many source bytes it is. Zero bytes for everything the
per-escape path has a diagnostic for -- a digit that is not one, a surrogate without its other
half -- which is therefore left exactly where it was. The caller keeps twelve bytes readable,
and five in front of `escape` when `p` is at least six.

A surrogate pair whose halves are both in the block is two escapes, six bytes each: the high
half checks the low one and decodes the pair, and the low half, recognised by the escape that
began six bytes back being a high surrogate (`second`), makes nothing. Every escape before it
in the block decoded, or the walk would have stopped, so that high half has already checked
this one's digits. Only a high half whose partner lies past the block takes twelve. Measured:
taking twelve at every pair made the walk clear the partner's bit from its mask with a `csel`
on `taken`, which put the whole decode -- two table lookups deep -- on the path to the next
escape's position; on `twitterescaped` that cost the walk 8% (161.7 against 149.5 us).

Unescape.c:stream_parsing_unescape_utf8.comment: A scalar's UTF-8 encoding little-endian in a word, and its length (`JSONParser.utf8Word`).
